wetland_management__asset_threat__drough.mechanism: Drought damages the restored wetland by taking away the water it runs on. In a rewetted Indonesian peat restoration area, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). The authors read their long record as showing that a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface, with carbon-emission spikes, even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and remaining peat-swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6). On a restored floodplain the hazard works by removing the flood the wetland depends on: in 2020, lack of snow cover and severe drought meant no spring flooding on the Pripyat floodplain, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly (ev_wgy_blr_6). The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to drought, as well as to fire, flooding and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_22).
wetland_management__asset_threat__drough.conditionality: Two of the four units are measurements — subsidence in Sumatra and bird numbers in a Belarus project evaluation; the other two are interpretation: the Hooijer authors' reading of their own record, and an expert statement with no frequency, site or measurement, made where the guidance itself notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. The Belarus case is floodplain meadow kept open by grazing and mowing, a different wetland type and practice from tropical peat rewetting, and its indicator is birds rather than any livelihood; the evaluation also names drought and snowless winters as arriving faster and more severely than the project was designed for. Settings are upper-middle-income Indonesia and Belarus plus guidance with no site; there is no low-income or lower-middle-income case. Design implication: a wetland investment in a drought-prone setting should budget and monitor for drought-year losses of peat surface, carbon, plantings and habitat function rather than treat them as failure of the works, and should expect the asset to deliver least in the dry years.

In a rewetted Indonesian peat restoration area, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). The authors read their long record as showing that a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface, with carbon-emission spikes, even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and remaining peat-swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6). wetland_management__asset_threat__drough.conditionality: One unit in each source is a measurement — subsidence in Sumatra, bird numbers in a Belarus project evaluation; the second Indonesian unit is the authors' reading of their own record rather than an independent measurement. The two cases are different wetland types and practices: canal-blocking rewetting of a retired pulpwood plantation on tropical peat, and floodplain meadows kept open by grazing and mowing on a temperate river, with birds rather than any livelihood as the indicator. The Belarus evaluation also names drought and snowless winters as arriving faster and more severely than the project was designed for. Both settings are upper-middle-income; the scope is in context for those, and nothing here was measured in a low-income or lower-middle-income country. Design implication: budget and monitor for drought-year losses of peat surface, carbon and habitat function rather than treat them as failure of the works, and expect the asset to deliver least in the dry years.

wetland_management__asset_threat__extrem.mechanism: The vulnerable asset is the canal dam that holds the water table up. In December 2005, after an extreme rainfall event, both dams in the Kalampangan Canal were damaged by water seeping underneath and along the sides; they were repaired in March 2006 and were damaged again in August 2006 (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_7). During an extreme rainfall event in August 2007 a further dam was damaged in a flash flood, the canal water level rising by several metres in a short period (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_8). The rainfall is the trigger; the vulnerability is structural, since highly permeable tropical peat lets seepage pass beneath and alongside a dam, and the sunken canals intercept overland and interflow, raising canal discharges when the rain is extreme.
wetland_management__asset_threat__extrem.conditionality: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.

wetland_management__asset_threat__fire.mechanism: Fire can destroy restoration plantings before they establish. The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to fire, as well as to flooding, drought and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_20).
wetland_management__asset_threat__fire.conditionality: One expert statement, with no site, frequency, area or measurement, made where the guidance notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting; it concerns tropical peat-swamp replanting only. It does not say whether the burned plantings were on rewetted or still-drained peat. It is a reason to budget for fire protection, replanting losses and replacement, not a measured rate of loss.

wetland_management__asset_threat__flood.mechanism: Flooding can destroy restoration plantings. The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to flooding, as well as to fire, drought and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_21).
wetland_management__asset_threat__flood.conditionality: One expert statement, with no site, frequency, area or measurement, made where the guidance notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. It does not say whether the flooding came from rivers or from the raised water table of rewetting itself, and it concerns tropical peat-swamp replanting only. It is a reason to budget for replanting losses and replacement, not a measured rate of loss.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: Restoring the hydrology and the vegetation of a drained or degraded wetland puts back the conditions a wetland biota needs — standing water, saturated soil, a vegetated surface — and species return from whatever source is in reach. Pooled across global meta-analysis, restoring degraded wetlands enhanced biodiversity by 19% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1], significantly for vertebrates (+53%), vascular plants (+45%) and terrestrial (+17%) and aquatic (+15%) invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3]. Creating wetlands in a farmed catchment works the same way from a lower base, by adding aquatic habitat to a landscape that has lost it: catchment-scale creation benefited the biodiversity of agricultural landscapes, particularly where the density of aquatic habitats was increased by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1], each additional created wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species to regional richness with a median of 2.70, and the accumulation curve had not flattened after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], so the regional species pool and its metapopulations keep gaining as more are built [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. What is done on the site matters as much as the water: a planted basin remained more diverse in plant cover 10 years after planting than an identical unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7], planting salt marsh improved biodiversity conservation against degraded wetland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_5], and active restoration or replacement measures are needed to speed up vegetation recolonisation on bare peat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_rasa23_10]. In the tropics, rewetting a retired pulpwood plantation left 57 native peat-swamp-forest tree species growing spontaneously, in high densities, in the most rewetted conditions [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3], and restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland is expected to enhance biodiversity alongside its other benefits [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4]. On the coast, reinstating tidal flow produced biodiversity gains in 57% of monitoring studies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1], and of the studies with species-specific data 77% reported positive effects on at least one commercially important fish species and 34% on invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_3]. Project reporting adds a European floodplain case: after the first test flooding of the restored Belene Island marshes on the Danube, park reports cited in the World Bank completion report record fish species rising from 2 to 10 within 2 months and ferruginous duck nesting pairs from 5 to 50, with mallard rising from 16 to 400 and rare birds such as purple heron and glossy ibis returning [ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1]; in Moldova a project-supported inventory found that flora and fauna began to regenerate after the Lapusna wetland was restored [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2]; and in Belarus, vegetation mapping after rewetting 950 ha of the Dokudovskoe cut-over peatland found Phragmites-sedge communities on at least 398 ha, against no more than 20 ha at baseline [ev_wgy_blr_7].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: The baseline is the degraded wetland, and that is what the gains are measured against. Where restored sites were compared with intact references they came close without matching: biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1], and the Swedish created wetlands were only almost as beneficial to biodiversity as mature reference ponds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. A shortfall against an intact reference is incomplete recovery, not harm done by the practice. The real harm in this row is elsewhere, and it is about how the restoration is done. Walking away from a degraded peatland is modelled as stagnating and even further deteriorating conditions more than 50 years after abandonment [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6], with Sphagnum recovery under passive restoration projected over centuries rather than decades [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5]; removing the stressor alone appeared to cause a decline in peatland specialist diversity, while enhanced restoration with active revegetation reached intact levels of that diversity within about 8 years, although the authors could not predict these responses with confidence [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_8]. On the coast, negative outcomes from tidal reinstatement were rare at 12% of studies reviewed, but one documented case had a non-native predator of the critically endangered native fish as the most abundant species at the restoration site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2]. Not every component responds: macroinvertebrate diversity showed no significant effect [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4], and macrobenthos abundance and biomass showed no major difference after salt-marsh planting [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7]. Two reading cautions. The tidal review counts an outcome as positive when it improves on the tidally restricted condition even if it does not reach a pristine reference, which its authors say may overestimate positive outcomes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1]; and the Sumatran regrowth is a bundled intervention — canal blocking together with clearing part of the plantation, on plots close to remaining forest that supplies the seed — so none of it is attributable to rewetting alone [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3]. Project evaluations need the same care. The Bulgarian figures are park reports relayed by the completion report and taken within months of the first flooding, so they show a fast early response, not a settled community [ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2]. The Belarus gain fell short of its own target of at least 700 ha, sedge seed was practically absent in the donor bogs for three years, and reed and cattail colonised first on most of the prepared area [ev_wgy_blr_7]. The low- and lower-middle-income units are thin and bundled: in Uzbekistan, wetlands formed on drainage collectors are said to offer adequate living conditions for fauna and flora on anecdotal evidence from site visits and committee reports, inside a bundled drainage and irrigation programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2]; and the Ugandan Green Climate Fund baseline found few significant differences in phytoplankton, green algae, flagellates, zooplankton and crustaceans between treatment and comparison wetland systems, a baseline comparison of a restoration bundled with access restrictions and livelihood support, not an impact estimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_fp034b_1]. Most of the evidence sits in high- and upper-middle-income countries across Europe, North America, Australia, China and Southeast Asia, so transfer to a low-income rural setting is an assumption, not a finding.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: On tropical peat, rewetting removes the drainage stress that keeps the site degraded, and where seed can still arrive the native community returns without planting: native peat-swamp-forest tree species were found growing spontaneously, at high density, in the most rewetted conditions of a restoration area (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peat is expected to deliver enhanced biodiversity alongside litter supply to the upper peat, a stabilised microclimate and reduced fire risk (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Neither unit isolates the practice, so this row carries direction and nothing about size or speed. The Sumatran observation is explicitly a best case: every plot lay close to remaining forest, so seed arrival is easy, and the regrowth cannot be separated from the earlier clearing or from that seed proximity - no share of the outcome is attributed to rewetting alone (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). The companion statement is a potential the authors expect, not a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4). Both come from upper-middle-income Southeast Asian peatlands, neither reports a comparison with an intact reference nor a time to recovery, and neither is from a low-income or farmed landscape - so for a humid-tropics scan this is a plausible-direction flag that needs local monitoring evidence before any magnitude is claimed, with distance to remaining forest the first thing to check on the ground.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In rainfed cropping landscapes the benefit comes from adding aquatic habitat where almost none remains. Catchment-scale wetland creation benefited the biodiversity of agricultural landscapes, particularly where the density of aquatic habitats rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each created wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness, with the accumulation curve still rising after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], and creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity in a landscape whose small waters had increased by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. Establishment choices last: the planted basin remained more diverse in plant cover 10 years after planting than its unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Both studies sit in temperate, high-income rainfed cropland, Sweden and Ohio, and neither is a restoration of a lost wetland: they are wetlands created under a programme designed and sited mainly for nutrient retention [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5] and a pair of pumped experimental basins [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. The 30% figure is a design condition on habitat density, not a measured effect size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]. The species gain is a regional accumulation across many wetlands, so it does not promise a gain at a single created site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3]. The Ohio comparison is planting against natural colonisation within created wetlands rather than wetland against no wetland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. Nothing here was measured in a tropical or low-income rainfed system, and no unit reports how the gain changes as the wetland ages.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In these high-income settings the gain comes from adding or re-making wetland habitat in landscapes that have lost it, and from working on the site rather than only on the water. Catchment-scale creation of dual-purpose wetlands benefited the biodiversity of agricultural landscapes, particularly where the density of aquatic habitats rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each new wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species to regional richness, median 2.70, with the species accumulation curve still climbing after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], so repeated creation keeps building the regional species pool and its metapopulations [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. On-site intervention adds to it: a planted basin was still more diverse in plant cover 10 years after planting than its unplanted twin [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7], salt-marsh planting improved biodiversity conservation relative to degraded wetland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_5], and on bare peat, active restoration or replacement measures are what speed vegetation recolonisation [ev_biodiversity_outcome_rasa23_10]. Reinstating tidal flow delivered biodiversity gains in 57% of monitoring studies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1], and among studies with species-specific data 77% reported positive effects on at least one commercially important fish species and 34% on invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_3]. Project reporting adds a European floodplain case: after the first test flooding of the restored Belene Island marshes on the Danube, park reports cited in the World Bank completion report record fish species rising from 2 to 10 within 2 months and ferruginous duck nesting pairs from 5 to 50, with mallard rising from 16 to 400 and rare birds such as purple heron and glossy ibis returning [ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: How the restoration is done decides the sign, and doing little is the losing option: passively restored peat sites are modelled as stagnating and even further deteriorating more than 50 years after abandonment [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6], Sphagnum recovery under passive restoration is projected over centuries rather than decades [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5], and stressor removal alone appeared to cause a decline in peatland specialist diversity where enhanced restoration with active revegetation reached intact levels within about 8 years — responses the authors could not predict with confidence [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_8]. Tidal reinstatement carried its own failure mode: negative outcomes were rare at 12% of studies, but in one case the most abundant fish at the restored site was a non-native predator of the critically endangered native fish the project set out to support [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2]. Parts of the biota did not move at all — macrobenthos abundance and biomass showed no major difference after planting [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7]. Read the positives with their comparators: the Swedish wetlands were almost as beneficial as mature reference ponds rather than equal to them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5], which is incomplete recovery against an intact reference and not a loss, since the comparison that matters for an investment is against the degraded or drained starting point; the tidal review counts an outcome as positive if it improves on the tidally restricted condition even when it falls short of a pristine reference, and says this may overestimate positive outcomes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1]; and the created-wetland contrast is planting against natural colonisation within created basins, not wetland against no wetland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. This row is scoped to the high-income evidence, which is where almost all of it was measured — Europe, North America and Australia — so it describes those contexts rather than transferring to them. The Bulgarian figures are park reports relayed by the completion report and taken within months of the first flooding, so they show a fast early response, not a settled community [ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2].

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: The only low- and lower-middle-income evidence describes wetlands that provide habitat where water is put back on the land. In the Amu Darya delta of Uzbekistan, wetlands formed on drainage collectors are reported, on anecdotal evidence from site visits and State Committee reports, to present adequate living conditions for fauna and flora and an adequate substitute for the drained eastern part of Lake Ayaskala [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Neither unit measures a change caused by the practice. The Uzbek claim is an evaluator's assertion resting on anecdote, and the wetlands it describes are a by-product of a bundled drainage-rerouting and irrigation programme in an irrigated cropping landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2]. The Ugandan Green Climate Fund evaluation is a baseline report: wetland systems showed few significant differences in phytoplankton, green algae, flagellates, zooplankton and crustaceans between treatment and comparison sites, which describes conditions at the start of a restoration bundled with access restrictions and alternative livelihood support, not its effect [ev_biodiversity_outcome_fp034b_1]. No unit gives a magnitude, and no unit measures vertebrates, plants or species of conservation concern in a low-income farmed landscape.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In upper-middle-income tropical peatland, the operative step is rewetting: removing the drainage stress lets the native community re-establish where a seed source remains, with native peat-swamp-forest tree species growing spontaneously and at high density in the most rewetted conditions (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peat is expected to enhance biodiversity alongside litter supply, microclimate stabilisation and reduced fire risk (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Although this row is in context for its income band, the pool behind it is very thin and neither unit isolates the practice. The field observation is a stated best case - plots lay close to remaining forest, and the regrowth is bundled with the earlier clearing and with seed proximity, with no share attributed to rewetting itself (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3); the companion claim is an expected benefit rather than a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4). Both are Indonesian and Malaysian peatlands, so the row speaks to tropical peat and not to other wetland types, to farmed landscapes, or to lower-income countries. No comparison with an intact reference and no recovery timescale is available here, so direction is all this supports; distance to intact forest is the first site-level check, and a monitoring commitment should accompany any investment scoped on it.

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: Only units that weigh carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide together can say which way the balance falls, and where they state one they favour rewetting over keeping the peat drained, along a time path. On a hundred-year global warming potential basis, rewetting drained organic soils gives net annual removals of carbon dioxide in the majority of organic soil classes, an increase in annual methane, a decrease in nitrous oxide and dissolved organic carbon, and a lowering of net greenhouse-gas emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1]; the same authors restate that rewetting strongly increases methane yet in general represents a significant climate-change mitigation action because of the considerable decrease in carbon dioxide and the accompanying nitrous-oxide reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_3]. The time path is the point to carry forward. The peatland-rewetting question-and-answer document, citing the literature, states that rewetting initially causes a slight warming impact because of increased methane, but that in the longer term the result is cooling [ev_wgy_qa_3, ev_wgy_qa_4]; the Ramsar technical report, also citing studies, holds that even where rewetting produces a disproportionally large initial methane peak the longer-term climate effects are much better than maintaining the drained status quo [ev_wgy_ram_3], and that the combined fluxes of carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and dissolved organic carbon are very positive for the climate compared with the former drained situation [ev_wgy_ram_1]. Scenario modelling traces the same path through radiative forcing: methane forcing does not undermine the mitigation potential of rewetting, while postponing it increases long-term warming through continued carbon dioxide emission [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_3]; total forcing reaches a plateau soon after rewetting because carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide are halted and methane is short-lived in the atmosphere [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_4]; the methane cost may temporarily be substantial but the carbon dioxide cost of inaction is much higher [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_5]; and the warming from methane plus nitrous oxide is fully compensated by carbon dioxide uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_3], with cumulative reductions of 583.8 and 782 tCO2eq per hectare under the modelled rewetting scenarios [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_1]. Field-based rates tie the balance to the water table: every 10 cm reduction in effective water-table depth reduces the net warming impact of carbon dioxide plus methane by at least 3 t CO2e per hectare per year until the depth is less than 30 cm [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1], and between 5 and 13 cm the cooling from carbon dioxide sequestration exceeds the warming from methane on a hundred-year horizon [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_5]. A German study cited in a Scottish evidence assessment found 17 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 saved by rewetting a reed-canary-grass peatland compared with its drained state, with no significant short-term effect of biomass harvest [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_1]; and a mesonetwork of restored wetlands on drained Californian peat showed that conversion can yield a net greenhouse-gas benefit over the original land use, but only in some cases [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_5]. Behind those balances sit the parts of the ledger. Both advocacy-adjacent documents assert the gas exchange plainly: rewetting stops carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide but re-installs methane [ev_wgy_qa_1, ev_wgy_qa_2], and will always lead to a reinstatement of methane emissions [ev_wgy_ram_2]. While the water table stays below the surface, emissions from peat oxidation fall roughly linearly as it is raised, so roughly half of them can be avoided by raising the table to half its former depth — a statement about the oxidation term alone, not the methane that appears near the surface [ev_wgy_ram_4]. Restoration also rebuilds stocks: aboveground biomass (SMD 2.52), belowground biomass (1.94) and soil carbon (0.62) rose, with carbon dioxide flux falling significantly (SMD −0.43) while methane rose (0.44) [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cama26_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_2].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: Water-table depth, climate zone and horizon decide whether the balance is a gain at all, and the methane term is where it turns. Where average water levels are raised above the peat surface, the net warming from higher methane is likely to exceed the cooling from the extra carbon dioxide sequestration over shorter time-horizons [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]: raising the water table from 30 to 0 cm adds roughly 7 t CO2e per hectare per year of methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_2], whereas stopping at 30 cm below the surface has a negligible influence on methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_3], and moderate rewetting to 10-20 cm below the surface is offered as the design that prevents a major portion of peat loss without causing high methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_6]. Climate zone splits the answer: in the tropics the cooling is immediate and almost linearly increasing because the methane rise offsets only a few per cent of it [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3], while in temperate and boreal agricultural peat the methane offsets a major part of the cooling for the first decades [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_4], and on forestry-drained peat the increased methane offsets over 100% of the cooling from reduced carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide for at least the first 40 years, and at least 50% even 100 years after rewetting [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5]; higher emissions were even estimated from rewetted temperate nutrient-rich forest sites than from their drained counterparts, which the authors call an apparent anomaly of their disaggregation [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_5]. Timing matters as much as place: carbon dioxide emissions decline soon after restoration whereas methane typically rises in the short term, with emerging evidence that the increase weakens as the ecosystem matures [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_11], individual studies report a methane peak in the first years [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_6], and in seagrass the only significant response to restoration was an increase in methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_10]. Even the global scenario that maximises mitigation nets out small: optimal re-wetting of peat cropland and grassland generates net carbon dioxide uptake of 106 Mt per year against an offsetting 91 Mt of methane, leaving a small net removal [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_6], while the less ambitious option of halving drainage depths cuts present-day carbon dioxide plus methane emissions by 65% [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_7]. The prior land use splits the answer as well: the Ramsar report, citing studies, states that rewetting tropical peat and agricultural peat outside the tropics always has a large and rapid mitigation effect, but that on boreal forestry-drained peat the effect may be much lower and slower, complicated by changing albedo and by substantial carbon dioxide emissions after clear-cutting [ev_wgy_ram_5]. Paludiculture and permanence carry their own limits. The 25-30 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 reduction quoted for paludiculture is mostly avoided emissions from deep-drained peat cropland, and the same assessment records that field experiments disagree on whether paludiculture sites become a net carbon dioxide sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_2]. Harvesting Sphagnum biomass is judged likely to prevent the peat from being a long-term carbon store and to cause further peat degradation — a review judgement, not a measurement, but a reversal for that form of paludiculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_3]. Converting rewetted peat back to agriculture is estimated to release 6.5 t C ha-1 yr-1 of additional emissions, a carbon-only figure for the loss side of the ledger [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_4]. And restored freshwater marshes that accrete soil carbon do so at the cost of significant methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_4]. Two further limits belong on this row. First, the strength rests on modelled scenarios rather than on measured net balances, and several units describe a single gas or a programme total and cannot carry a net claim. The Belarus terminal evaluation estimates emissions of 7.1 tons per ha per year after rewetting and 4.9 after 20 years, and reports a 65 % reduction against baseline with 75 % anticipated after 20 years; the evaluation calls these greenhouse-gas emissions, but the estimates are carbon dioxide only, no methane is reported, and they are modelled, so they describe the carbon dioxide part of the ledger, not a net balance [ev_wgy_blr_3, ev_wgy_blr_4]. Indonesia's Peatland Restoration Agency attributes a reduction of approximately 285 million tons of CO2eq to water-management improvement, derived from a water-level monitoring database rather than from measured fluxes [ev_carbon_sequestration_cifor270_1]. The measured units are mostly single-gas: restoration decreased soil carbon dioxide emission and increased methane against the unrestored extraction site, both rising with a higher water table and more vascular plant cover [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2]; a British gully-blocking restoration changed neither photosynthesis nor ecosystem respiration while methane was significantly greater in the sparsely vegetated rewetted pans [ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null, ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up]; and in Sumatra the carbon case is read off subsidence, halved where water tables were raised, implying an emission reduction of 6.4 to 23.6 Mg per hectare per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1]. Each of those describes a part of the ledger, not the balance. Second, a rewetted site is not an intact one: at an Irish rewetted peatland the carbon dioxide emission factor fell significantly but methane stayed above natural sites, and after a decade of rewetting the global warming potential of the rewetted sites was still higher than intact peatlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]. That is incomplete recovery against an intact reference; the gain claimed here is against the drained, degraded starting point, and on tropical plantation peat even full water-table control was modelled to cut emissions by no more than 20% of what drainage currently causes [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1]. The country-bearing evidence is northern-European, Canadian, Irish, Estonian, Belarusian, Californian and Indonesian; the tropical results that carry the largest mitigation are modelled [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_7].

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: In the humid tropics every unit in this pool is one side of the greenhouse-gas ledger, and no source weighs the sides against each other. On the carbon dioxide side, rewetting drained tropical peat slows subsidence and the peat decomposition it indicates [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_1], with a stated ceiling on what in-plantation water management can buy back [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1] and a drained-forest case where raising the water level hardly reduced the surface flux because root respiration dominates [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_2]. On the methane side, the paired Kalimantan sites show fluxes moving in opposite directions after damming, with the authors reading the overall effect on the annual methane budget as small [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5]. Vegetation regrowth on open restored peat is reported as still too small to compensate for carbon losses from decomposition [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_3].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: No class is stated because no unit here reports a net carbon dioxide equivalent balance: the subsidence-based accounting integrates the gases without separating them, the flux studies report one gas at a time, and the question that decides the class — whether methane gains exceed the carbon dioxide saved — is unanswered for tropical sites. One source states the gap outright for the field as a whole. A single measured net balance from a rewetted tropical site would let this cell state a class; until then the carbon dioxide savings and the methane movements sit side by side [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_6].

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: In high-income temperate and boreal settings the mechanism is measured directly against the water table. Every 10 cm the effective water-table depth is raised cuts the net warming of carbon dioxide plus methane together by at least 3 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1, on a stated hundred-year global warming potential basis, until the table is within 30 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]; between 5 and 13 cm depth the cooling from carbon dioxide sequestration exceeds the warming from methane, giving a small net cooling on that horizon [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_5]. Halving drainage depths while the land stays in production cuts global carbon dioxide plus methane emissions by 65%, methane staying under 5 Mt CO2e yr-1 precisely because the table is not taken to the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_7], worth 15.3 t CO2 ha-1 yr-1 on cropland organic soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_9]. On cutaway peat, restoration decreased soil carbon dioxide emission and raised net carbon dioxide uptake where the water table and vascular cover were higher [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1]; carbon dioxide losses fell after Canadian cutaway peat was restored and Finnish peatlands became a new sink within a few years [ev_carbon_sequestration_erwi09_1]; a rewetted Irish site had a significantly reduced carbon dioxide emission factor of 104 g CO2-C m-2 yr-1, the sign indicating net uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]; and reed canary grass plots on cutover peat had lower global warming potential than bare peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_5]. In coastal and created systems the stock terms move as well: planting raised soil organic carbon by 10.70 Mg C ha-1 against adjacent degraded wetland [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4], organic matter in created-wetland surface soils rose by about 1% per 3-year period [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], and nitrous oxide fluxes were lower when marsh and edge plots were inundated [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. Rewetting also reduces the carbon dioxide and nitrous-oxide emissions of peat drained for agriculture and forestry [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_2], and shallow lakes created on peat-extraction sites can reduce net greenhouse-gas flux through carbon sequestration [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: Prior land use decides the sign more sharply in this pool than anywhere. On temperate and boreal agricultural peat the warming from methane offsets a major part of the cooling for the first decades after rewetting [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_4]; on forestry-drained peat the increased methane offsets over 100% of the cooling from decreased carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide for at least the first 40 years, and still at least 50% a century later, while rewetting also decreases the carbon stored in the trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_1]. Taking the water table from 30 cm depth to the surface adds roughly 7 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 of methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_2], where stopping at 30 cm has a negligible effect, at most 0.3 [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_3]; raising water above the peat surface is expected to warm over shorter horizons [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]; and moderate rewetting to 10-20 cm below the surface is the design that keeps both gases on the right side [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_6]. An upland English rewetting shows the trade-off unhedged: methane from the sparsely vegetated rewetted pans was significantly greater than from the vegetated haggs [ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up], while photosynthesis and ecosystem respiration did not change, so the carbon dioxide side did not offset it [ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null]. Rewetting cutaway peat likewise increased methane as it cut carbon dioxide, both driven by the same higher water table and vascular cover [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2], and after a decade some restored sites still showed a more warming balance and higher sensitivity to climate anomalies than intact peatland [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_3]. In created riverine wetlands methane rose significantly once flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, though average emission from pulsed sites stayed below permanently flooded sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8], the nitrous oxide benefit did not extend to upland plots [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10], and the created shallow lakes caused methane emissions even while offering a net flux reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_9]. Because there is no variable for an individual gas, the carbon dioxide fall and the methane rise in these sources enter the pool with opposite signs; the sources themselves largely agree on the net direction. The scale figures are modelled rather than measured, and the tropical rows of that model are extrapolated from these temperate and boreal relationships, not observed [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_8]. Everything here sits outside the low- and lower-middle-income target: the measured sites are in the UK, Ireland, Canada, Finland, Estonia, the USA and China, and nothing in this scope row measures a tropical peat system.

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: This row rests on the drainage side of the ledger: it is mostly an account of the carbon that drained wetlands lose, and of the expectation that putting the water back stops the loss. Drained peatlands release 645 Mt C per year through soil respiration, approximately 5% of global annual anthropogenic carbon emissions [ev_wetflA_ma_global_release], and the driver is the water table itself — its decline stimulated heterotrophic rather than autotrophic soil respiration and was associated with an increase in subsidence rate, a relationship that held across climate zones and land uses [ev_wetflA_ma_wt_respiration]. The loss is largest where the peat is warm: drained tropical peatlands under different land uses respire an estimated 10,865 to 23,685 kg C per hectare per year, the highest of any zone or land use in that synthesis [ev_wetflA_ma_tropical_rates], and degraded peatlands as a whole emit 2 Gt CO2 per year, nearly a quarter of land-sector emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_bonn16_2]. Reversing the driver is where the positive direction comes from: restoring degraded hydric soils and ecosystems is given a high potential for sequestering soil carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2], because carbon storage is enhanced under the anoxic conditions that flooded wetlands restore, which favour the accretion of organic matter [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3], and compared to degraded sites restored peatlands have lower carbon emission rates and over time can become net carbon sinks [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: Nothing in this row weighs methane against carbon dioxide, so it cannot say what the net greenhouse-gas balance of rewetting is, or over what horizon. The units are either loss-frame estimates of what drainage costs or statements of sequestration potential, and the restoration-side units are expert and review assertions rather than measured rates: a high potential, an anoxic mechanism, and a direction of travel over unspecified time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3, ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1]. Scarcely any of the same-direction units say how big the effect is, which is why the row states a direction and not a size. The tropical rate is the rate of loss under drainage, not a measured recovery after rewetting [ev_wetflA_ma_tropical_rates], and the global totals are not per-hectare effect sizes for an investment [ev_wetflA_ma_global_release, ev_carbon_sequestration_bonn16_2]. The scope is the pooled, multi-country evidence rather than any named country, so there is no national or agro-ecological context attached to it; treat it as the carbon-dioxide and soil-carbon side of the case, to be read alongside the rows that carry the methane term.

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: In the upper-middle-income pool, dominated by Indonesian and Malaysian peat, every unit is one side of the ledger. Rewetting slows subsidence and the decomposition it indicates [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_1], paludiculture rewetting cuts carbon dioxide from the peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1], a national monitoring programme attributes a large emission reduction to restoration on the carbon dioxide side [ev_carbon_sequestration_cifor270_1], and the Belarus pilots report per-hectare carbon dioxide reductions with no methane term [ev_wgy_blr_3, ev_wgy_blr_4]. The methane side moves the other way where it is measured at all: the carbon dioxide reduction under paludiculture may be offset by rising methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_2], and the Kalimantan flux pairs point in opposite directions [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: No class is stated because none of these sources weighs the gases against each other: the scenario figure is a carbon dioxide equivalent whose composition is not given [ev_carbon_sequestration_alex26_2], the Belarus indicator is labelled greenhouse gas but every figure is carbon dioxide only, and the subsidence accounting integrates gases without separating them. Whether methane gains exceed the carbon dioxide saved is exactly the question this cell cannot yet answer; vegetation uptake on open restored peat is also reported as too small to offset decomposition [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_2].

wetland_management__coastal__asset_threa.mechanism: What wears a salt marsh away is the ordinary wave climate, not the cyclone. A global analysis of salt-marsh erosion and wave measurements found that most salt-marsh deterioration is caused by moderate storms of monthly frequency (ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_6), while intense hurricanes contribute less than 1% to long-term salt-marsh erosion rates (ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_5) — the marsh survives the violent event and is eroded between them.
wetland_management__coastal__asset_threa.conditionality: Both units are drawn from the same sentence of the same review reporting the same global dataset, so this is a single line of evidence. It concerns lateral erosion of the marsh edge and no other failure mode, and it describes established marsh rather than a newly planted or recently restored one, where edge stability is likely to be weakest. The review's accompanying point is that retreat scales with wave energy rather than switching on above a critical storm, so the maintenance burden is continuous rather than event-driven: budget for steady edge retreat under the everyday wave climate rather than for post-cyclone repair. Provenance is high-income North Atlantic and European coasts.

wetland_management__coastal__biodiversit.mechanism: Replanting marsh vegetation or reinstating tidal exchange rebuilds the habitat structure and the inundation regime that coastal species depend on. Against degraded or tidally restricted conditions this registers as a biodiversity gain in most monitoring studies and in the pooled planting analysis (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_5), with mobile and commercially relevant taxa responding most: birds were more abundant in planted marsh than in nearby natural marsh, and most studies with species-level data reported positive effects on at least one commercially important fish species (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_14, ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_3). Protection of existing coastal lagoons in Ghana points the same way on birds: at the Keta Ramsar site the number of waders increased from about 31,400 in 1986 to 96,661 in 1998, as cited from waterbird monitoring by the wildlife authority [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ghicr_1], and the later evaluation judges that the rate of decline was on average slowed [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ghppar_1].
wetland_management__coastal__biodiversit.conditionality: The direction holds against a degraded or tidally restricted baseline and not against an intact one. Restored marshes carried significantly lower vegetation species richness than natural marshes, and lower macrobenthos richness with it (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_13), so the plant community that defines the habitat is the part that does not come back - while birds and fishery species do (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_14). A scoping read must keep the intact and degraded comparisons apart rather than netting them. Non-response and harm are both recorded: macrobenthos abundance and biomass showed no major difference from degraded wetland (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7), and a small share of tidal-reinstatement studies reported negative outcomes, including a restored site whose most abundant fish was a non-native predator of the critically endangered native fish the project set out to support (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2). Most units are shares of studies or effect sizes rather than measured magnitudes, and the tidal review states that counting an outcome positive whenever it improves on the restricted condition may overstate positive results (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1). The Ghanaian units describe protection of existing lagoon sites, not restoration, and the comparator is an earlier count at the same site: the wader rise is a cited monitoring figure, an earlier count against a later one with no control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ghicr_1], and the independent evaluation qualifies it — the integrity of these wetlands remains under threat despite the project, upstream degradation from agriculture, logging and urbanisation upsets their hydrological and nutrient balance, and their subsequent health cannot be determined for lack of monitoring [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ghppar_1]. Outside Ghana the evidence is high-income coastal, dominated by the United States, with planting dominated by a single genus.

wetland_management__coastal__carbon_sequ.mechanism: Coastal restoration works through carbon stocks rather than through the peat gas balance. Planting salt marsh increased soil carbon storage against degraded wetlands (effect size 0.21), alongside gains in shoreline protection, primary productivity, biodiversity and fishery production [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4], and raised soil organic carbon stocks by 10.70 +/- 3.45 Mg C per hectare relative to adjacent degraded wetlands, with aboveground and belowground biomass up 237.88 and 479.18 g per square metre [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6]. Measured against a natural marsh rather than a degraded baseline, restored marshes matched the reference on carbon dioxide flux (Hedges' g* = 0.03, n = 86, not significant) and on soil organic carbon accumulation rate (64.26 against 64.72 g per square metre per year, n = 18), and emitted significantly less methane (g* = -0.21, n = 70) [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11, ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]. In saline systems sulphate suppresses methanogenesis, so the methane penalty that dominates freshwater rewetting is largely absent here.
wetland_management__coastal__carbon_sequ.conditionality: The negative direction of this row rests on a single subgroup result in a single preprint: among wetland types, seagrass showed only a significant increase in methane flux, with no offsetting significant benefit [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_10]. That result is real and is not hidden, but it carries the row against the salt-marsh findings because it is weighted as a meta-analysis, while its own authors note that seagrass beds were under-represented in the dataset and that tropical and southern regions are a major geographical gap. Seagrass and salt marsh are not interchangeable, and the only methane result in salt marsh points the other way [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]. Comparator matters too: the gains are measured against degraded wetland, which is the counterfactual a restoration project faces [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6], while the equivalence results are measured against natural marsh and say that restored marshes accumulate carbon as fast as natural ones even while their stocks lag [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11]. The salt-marsh evidence is high-income and overwhelmingly North American, European and East Asian, with planting dominated by a single genus, and some plantings also received fertiliser or protective structures [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6]. Nothing in this row is a tropical mangrove or a low- or lower-middle-income coastal system, and no unit states a net balance over a stated horizon.

wetland_management__coastal__cost_per_he.mechanism: Every unit in this row comes from the same global salt-marsh review, which reports project budgets divided by the area restored. Mean total cost per hectare at unprotected sites is USD 495,067-876,564 in middle-income countries [ev_project_cost_wang22_1] and USD 454,285-694,724 in high-income countries [ev_project_cost_wang22_2]. Broken out by method, within the middle-income unprotected cell, hydrological restoration costs USD 6,090-9,945 per hectare [ev_project_cost_wang22_3] while vegetation restoration costs USD 26,945-42,756 [ev_project_cost_wang22_4]. What a coastal project does therefore drives its cost far more than where it is done.
wetland_management__coastal__cost_per_he.conditionality: A single source carries the whole row, so there is no cross-source check on it. The headline per-hectare totals are flagged by the compilers as implausibly high for a landscape intervention: project areas are small and the budgets include engineering, hard structures and land, so the ordinal reading (coastal restoration is expensive, and hydrological work is its cheapest component) is what transfers, not the number. The quoted ranges are the spread across the review's alternative monetary conversion methods, not confidence intervals. The evidence base is China, Great Britain, the Netherlands and the United States; it is not a low- or lower-middle-income cost, and tidal and marsh engineering costs should not be carried to inland or smallholder settings.

wetland_management__coastal__cost_reduct.mechanism: Both units come from the same global tidal-reinstatement review and both describe cost rising, not falling. Tidal reinstatement is often more cost-intensive than other types of coastal wetland restoration because it requires hydrological engineering, land acquisition, feasibility assessments, spatial modelling and complex regulatory compliance and permits [ev_project_cost_tidal26_5]. Reported project costs vary widely with scale and setting: Colombia's Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta at 128,000 ha cost US$20.1 million, against US$1.17 million for the 38 ha Galilee Saltmarsh Restoration in the United States [ev_project_cost_tidal26_4].
wetland_management__coastal__cost_reduct.conditionality: A single source carries the row, and it reports project totals with no comparable per-hectare denominator, so the two schemes cannot be put on the same scale without arithmetic the source does not perform. Nothing here measures avoided or reduced cost, so the target name overstates what the pool contains. The reviewed projects are concentrated in the United States, Australia and England, with Colombia the sole upper-middle-income case, and the review's own emphasis is that government funding is what carries the upfront cost — a condition that cannot be assumed in a low- or lower-middle-income investment.

wetland_management__coastal__flood__all.mechanism: Salt marsh dissipates wave energy and takes height off a surge as it travels across the platform. Wave heights fall by 72% across salt marsh, with a 95% confidence interval of 62 to 79% in a meta-analysis of field measurements (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1); up to 82% of wave energy is dissipated over marsh against 29% over the adjacent sand flat (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_3); storm-surge attenuation rates run from 1.7 to 25 cm per kilometre of marsh depending on marsh and storm characteristics (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_1). The vegetated-versus-unvegetated contrast is consistent — salt marsh vegetation had a significant positive effect on wave attenuation, and every paired study comparing vegetated marsh with intertidal mudflat concluded attenuation is greater over the marsh (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_1, ev_flood_hazard_shep11_2).
wetland_management__coastal__flood__all.conditionality: What has been measured is wave attenuation under ordinary conditions: the meta-analysed measurements are all taken under normal conditions of low waves (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1). The function weakens exactly where protection is wanted — attenuation works less effectively during extreme storms lasting more than a day, which the review reads as a reason not to rely on nature-based flood defences alone in populated low-lying coastal and estuarine areas (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_2). Floodwater attenuation inside the marsh, meaning flood-peak reduction and floodwater storage, has never been quantified: the systematic review found no study evaluating it (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_5). Siting can cancel the benefit, since levees and dikes behind a marsh cause water to set up against the structure and limit the surge-attenuating effect (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_4). The remaining support is self-reported: 41% of salt-marsh projects state that such habitats provide improved protection from storm events (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). Provenance: existing marsh rather than restored marsh, on high-income US, UK, Dutch, Belgian, Italian and Vietnamese coasts, with coastal property and society as the beneficiary rather than the farm.
