wetland_management__coastal__rural_pover.mechanism: The entire row is coastal protection economics. Salt-marsh nature-based defences carry a replacement cost ratio against a submerged breakwater averaging 2 (0.95-3.01) [ev_economic_return_nara16_3], with marsh projects running from just as expensive to around three times cheaper than the engineered alternative depending on water depth [ev_economic_return_nara16_6], although the same review states the defences are not always cost effective [ev_economic_return_nara16_5]. About 40% of salt-marsh restoration projects recover their investment cost within 30 years [ev_economic_return_wang22_5], and adding carbon sequestration value shortens the recovery period at both the low and the high carbon price tested [ev_economic_return_wang22_6].
wetland_management__coastal__rural_pover.conditionality: This row does not measure poverty, income or any household outcome; the beneficiary in every unit is society, and the benefits are avoided storm damage, avoided engineering cost and, in part, modelled carbon value. The cost recovery share excludes maintenance and running costs and rests on benefit data covering only a couple of ecosystem services, both of which push the share up; the replacement cost ratio spans the no-difference value and is recorded as not significant. The evidence is from China, Great Britain, the Netherlands, the United States and Vietnam, almost entirely high-income, while the target is low- and lower-middle-income. Read the class as a statement that coastal wetland projects can compete with hard engineering on cost where protected assets are valuable, and not as a statement that they lift rural households out of poverty.

wetland_management__coastal__soil_erosio.mechanism: Marsh vegetation attenuates waves and currents as water passes through the canopy, so suspended sediment settles, the bed accretes and surface elevation is maintained while lateral erosion of the shoreline is reduced. That mechanism is measured from both ends: inside existing marsh against adjacent unvegetated mudflat, where most paired studies reported increased accretion or surface elevation or reduced erosion and the pooled effect on shoreline stabilisation was positive (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4); and in planted marsh, which improved shoreline protection against degraded wetland (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3) and trapped sediment at least as well as the adjacent natural marsh (ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15).
wetland_management__coastal__soil_erosio.conditionality: Much of the pool is not a restoration result at all: the paired-study evidence measures what EXISTING marsh does against bare mudflat (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4), which is an argument for protecting marsh that is already there rather than a measured gain from creating or replanting it, and a sizeable minority of those paired studies did not report a positive effect. The planted-versus-natural trapping estimate is hedged by its own authors (ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15), and the restored-versus-degraded pooled values are effect sizes and shares of studies whose scale the sources do not define (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3), which is why direction is firmer than magnitude here. This is shoreline and tidal-flat erosion only - it carries nothing about soil loss from cropland or rangeland - and the field sites are high-income coasts in the United States, United Kingdom, China and the Netherlands, with the authors noting that matched restored and degraded pairs are few.

wetland_management__coastal__water_quali.mechanism: A planted salt-marsh canopy slows tidal flow and waves, so suspended particles and the nutrients and contaminants bound to them drop out of the water column and are trapped in the marsh instead of moving on. The measured expression of that here is sediment trapping by planted marsh, which matched or bettered the adjacent natural marsh (ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15).
wetland_management__coastal__water_quali.conditionality: The row rests on a single meta-analytic estimate that its own authors hedge, and the comparison is against adjacent NATURAL marsh - so it says a planted marsh traps sediment at least as well as an intact one, not what the gain is over an unvegetated shore or over doing nothing. Sediment trapping is also a proxy for particulate and turbidity load, not a measurement of nutrient or contaminant removal; nothing in this pool measures nitrogen or phosphorus. The underlying studies are concentrated in North America, Europe and East Asia and are high-income coastal settings, with no observation from a low- or lower-middle-income farmed catchment, and the practice is marsh planting dominated by a single genus - a different intervention from the inland nutrient-retention wetlands that carry the main water-quality case.

wetland_management__coastal__wind_cyclon.mechanism: Coastal wetland standing between a cyclone and exposed property reduces the damage done, measured as an elasticity across US Atlantic and Gulf coastal counties: a 1% loss of coastal wetlands is associated with a 0.6% increase in property damage (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_1). Valued at the margin, the median county's wetland is worth about $91,000 per km2 per year in storm protection, against an average of about $1.8 million and a range from less than $800 to $100 million per km2 (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_4), and a counterfactual on a single hurricane put the damage attributable to prior wetland loss at about $430 million (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_5).
wetland_management__coastal__wind_cyclon.conditionality: Protection is proportionately smallest where the storm is strongest: the elasticity of property damage with respect to wetlands is 0.58 for a tropical storm and 0.35 for a category 3 to 5 hurricane (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_2, ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_3). Built defences substitute for it — the elasticity is 0.50 in states with stricter building codes against 0.81 where codes and enforcement are weaker (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_6). All of this is measured on existing wetland cover rather than on a restoration project, and the same authors warn that a replacement wetland may take decades to fully develop the functions of the wetland it replaces (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_7), so the measured value is not what a new project delivers. Provenance: a single US panel study of high-income coastal counties; the outcome is damage to coastal property, a societal and asset-owner benefit rather than a rural livelihood one, and nothing in the cell speaks to a low-income or lower-middle-income coast.

wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: Cost per hectare is set mainly by what the restoration has to build. Re-establishing water flows is the cheap end: Indonesia's national canal-blocking programme is estimated at US$2,300/ha [ev_wgy_ram_19] and peatland restoration there at an average of around USD1,866 ha-1 [ev_project_cost_alex26_1]; controlled flooding of former Danube marshes in Bulgaria came in at US$1,903/ha at completion against US$2,145/ha at appraisal [ev_project_cost_bgieg_1]; wetland revegetation in Vermont is costed at $3200 ha-1 against $6400 ha-1 for forest revegetation [ev_project_cost_gour20_5]. Planting and hard engineering are the expensive end: in the salt marsh review, hydrological restoration at unprotected middle-income sites cost 6,090 to 9,945 $/ha against 26,945 to 42,756 $/ha for vegetation restoration [ev_project_cost_wang22_3, ev_project_cost_wang22_4], and whole-project means run to 454,285 to 694,724 $/ha at unprotected high-income sites [ev_project_cost_wang22_2].
wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: No cost figure comes from a low- or lower-middle-income country, so these numbers orient rather than transfer. They are not comparable with each other: some are programme estimates with no price year (Indonesia), some exclude land (the Vermont easement is costed separately), and the salt marsh means are total project cost divided by small restored areas, including engineering and land. Read them ordinally: large-area hydrological rewetting sits in the low thousands of US dollars per hectare, small engineered coastal projects orders of magnitude higher. The engine states no value range because the contract gates do not pass.

wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: In high-income settings the per-hectare cost depends on scale and on how much engineering and land the project buys. The Bulgarian Danube floodplain project restored 4,035 ha against a target of 2,340 ha, at US$1,903/ha at completion versus US$2,145/ha at appraisal [ev_project_cost_bgieg_1]; NRCS unit costs put wetland revegetation at $3200 ha-1 in Vermont [ev_project_cost_gour20_5]; unprotected salt marsh projects in high-income countries average 454,285 to 694,724 $/ha [ev_project_cost_wang22_2].
wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: The moderate cost class rests on the Bulgarian figure, the only quantified unit that passed the band rule; the stated range spans several orders of magnitude because the salt marsh figure is total project cost over small coastal sites. Valid for high-income contexts only; the Vermont figure is a model input that excludes the land easement, and no source gives a currency year.

wetland_management__cost_reduction.mechanism: Restoration costs are pushed up by engineering, land and regulation rather than brought down: tidal reinstatement is described as more cost-intensive than other coastal restoration because it needs hydrological engineering, land acquisition, feasibility work, spatial modelling and permits [ev_project_cost_tidal26_5]. Scale matters: Colombia's Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta (128,000 ha) cost US$20.1 million, while a 38 ha US saltmarsh project cost US$1.17 million [ev_project_cost_tidal26_4]. For wet farming on rewetted peat, specialised harvesting equipment and adapted production raise investment cost and risk above the drained baseline [ev_wet_cost_neud26_3]; Sphagnum farming establishment, calculated from pilot cost data in 2011 and again in 2016, fell between the dates but stayed in the order of a hundred thousand euros per hectare of production field [ev_wgy_wich_7].
wetland_management__cost_reduction.conditionality: The evidence is almost entirely high-income (US, European and Australian projects); nothing here shows restoration lowering farm or project costs. The Sphagnum figures fall between the two dates but stay far above conventional land use, and they are for a high-input pilot. Do not read the absence of cost-reduction evidence as proof that low-cost community-based rewetting in low-income settings cannot be cheap; it is simply not in the pool.

wetland_management__creation__biodiversi.mechanism: Creating wetlands in farmland adds habitat that the landscape has lost, and the new basins can reach the standard of the old ones. Dual-purpose created wetlands sustained alpha, beta and gamma diversity similar to that of natural lentic water bodies in the region [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2], and the pollution-sensitive stoneflies, mayflies and caddisflies made up almost twice as large a share of richness in the created wetlands, 19%, as in the reference ponds, 10% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_4]. Catchment-scale creation benefited landscape biodiversity, particularly where aquatic habitat density rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each new wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness with no asymptote after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], so creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity where small waters had risen by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. Planting at creation left a lasting mark: the planted basin was still more diverse in plant cover 10 years on than the unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. In the Amu Darya delta of Uzbekistan, wetlands formed on drainage collectors are reported to present adequate living conditions for fauna and flora and an adequate substitute for the drained part of Lake Ayaskala [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2].
wetland_management__creation__biodiversi.conditionality: Most of these findings state a direction without an effect size. Two of the strongest results are comparisons against mature natural ponds rather than against a no-wetland baseline, so they say the created wetlands are as good as the existing ones, not how much the landscape gained by building them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_4]. The measured evidence is temperate and high-income, Sweden and Ohio, and the Swedish wetlands were designed and sited mainly for nutrient retention [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]. The species gain is regional and cumulative, not a promise for a single basin [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3]. The Ohio contrast is planting against natural colonisation inside created wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. The one lower-income unit, from Uzbekistan, is an evaluator's statement resting on anecdotal site visits and committee reports, about wetlands that arose within a bundled drainage and irrigation programme rather than being built for habitat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2]; no tropical or lower-income measurement is present, and no unit reports whether the invertebrate advantage holds as the wetlands age and fill with sediment.

wetland_management__creation__carbon_seq.mechanism: Creating a wetland builds a new carbon store from scratch. In created riverine basins in Ohio, organic matter in surface soils increased by approximately 1% per 3-year period over the decade after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], and nitrous oxide fluxes from marsh and edge plots were lower when those plots were inundated than when the same plots were exposed to air [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. Shallow lakes created on former peat-extraction sites had the potential to reduce net greenhouse-gas flux through carbon sequestration [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].
wetland_management__creation__carbon_seq.conditionality: The methane cost of putting water onto land sits in the same sources. Methane emission from vegetated areas rose significantly when flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, although average emission from pulsed sites stayed below that of permanently flooded sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8], and the created shallow lakes caused methane emissions to the atmosphere even as they offered a net flux reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_9]. The nitrous oxide benefit reaches only as far as the water does: in the upland plots, fluxes did not differ between flooded and dry periods [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10]. Because the register has no variable for an individual gas, the carbon dioxide and nitrous-oxide gains and the methane rise from the same experiment enter the pool with opposite signs, which makes the evidence look more divided than it is: both sources report a net gain with a methane penalty inside it. The row rests on a pair of pumped experimental basins in temperate Ohio and a review of boreal and northern European peat-extraction after-use. No unit states a net balance over any horizon, none measures how the balance changes as the created wetland matures, and none is from a low- or lower-middle-income setting [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].

wetland_management__creation__flood__all.mechanism: Created storage intercepts part of the storm volume before it reaches the receptor: the review reports that reduction of peak discharge by online and offline storage areas is effective and notable in both fieldwork and modelling results (ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective), online storage being blocking within the drainage network and offline storage being retention and detention features set aside from the channel.
wetland_management__creation__flood__all.conditionality: That sentence is the entire evidence base for this cell, and the review qualifies it in the same breath: the location of offline storage features is the most important factor, depending on soil type and on the number and spatial distribution of the features in the catchment (ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective). A creation programme that does not site its features deliberately has no claim on this result. There is no measured outcome for a created wetland here, no second source, and nothing on how the effect behaves as events get rarer. Provenance: UK and European studies, temperate and high-income, so transfer to a tropical or smallholder catchment is an assumption rather than a finding, and the benefit is downstream rather than on the plot.

wetland_management__creation__flood_haza.mechanism: Created storage intercepts part of the storm volume before it reaches the receptor: the review reports that reduction of peak discharge by online and offline storage areas is effective and notable in both fieldwork and modelling results (ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective), online storage being blocking within the drainage network and offline storage being retention and detention features set aside from the channel.
wetland_management__creation__flood_haza.conditionality: That sentence is the entire evidence base for this cell, and the review qualifies it immediately: the location of offline storage features is the most important factor, depending on soil type and on the number and spatial distribution of the features in the catchment (ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective). A creation programme that does not site its features deliberately has no claim on the result. There is no measured outcome for a created wetland here, no second source, and nothing on how the effect behaves as events get rarer. Provenance: UK and European, temperate and high-income, so transfer to a tropical or smallholder catchment is an assumption rather than a finding, and the benefit is downstream rather than on the plot.

wetland_management__creation__rural_pove.mechanism: In Karakalpakstan, saline drainage effluent rerouted through new collectors formed wetlands along them, and the project completion report credits the revival of fish, muskrat skin and reed production from these wetlands with a substantial increase in income for residents [ev_household_income_uzicr_1].
wetland_management__creation__rural_pove.conditionality: A single self-evaluation that did not directly measure income, from a bundled drainage and irrigation project; it cannot set a direction. The created wetlands are a by-product of drainage rerouting, not a deliberate wetland-creation investment. A measured household outcome would be needed before this family carries a poverty class.

wetland_management__creation__soil_erosi.mechanism: A created wetland traps sediment by slowing the water crossing it, and that capacity is finite: as the basin fills, sediment-bound material begins to pass through or discharge again. In the created riverine basins there were signs that sediment and total-phosphorus retention were diminishing after a decade of continuous river flow, while nitrate and soluble-reactive-phosphorus retention persisted (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5) - the sediment function ages out faster than the nitrogen function.
wetland_management__creation__soil_erosi.conditionality: Read the adverse sign narrowly. The row rests on a single narrative statement from a single pair of created basins, and what was observed is a declining sediment-RETENTION service, not measured erosion of land; the authors themselves put it as 'some signs'. It does not say that creating a wetland causes soil loss, only that the trapping benefit should not be assumed to persist without sediment management or maintenance, which belongs in the cost and operations case rather than in the opportunity surface. The setting is a temperate rainfed cropping catchment in a high-income country, pumped continuously from a river, so neither the sediment load nor the maintenance regime transfers to a low- or lower-middle-income landscape without local evidence.

wetland_management__creation__water_qual.mechanism: A created wetland works as a reactor placed in the flow path: residence time rises, nitrogen is removed by plant uptake and denitrification and phosphorus settles with sediment, so a share of the incoming load leaves the water. Across created and restored freshwater wetlands that is a measured net removal of total nitrogen and total phosphorus, both as mass rates and as a share of the incoming load (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_1, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_2, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_4, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_5), and nitrate and soluble-reactive-phosphorus retention persisted into the tenth year of a created riverine pair (ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3). Where new wetlands are put matters more than how many: modelled placement in the highest nitrogen-surplus areas removes far more nitrogen than placement on non-agricultural land, at a higher cost because it takes cropland out of production (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3), and the gain flattens as restoration spreads beyond the hotspots (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_5). Created wetlands can be designed to hold nutrients and carry species diversity at the same time rather than trading them off (ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6).
wetland_management__creation__water_qual.conditionality: Creating a wetland on nutrient-enriched farmland can reverse the sign. Negative phosphorus removal - the wetland exporting phosphorus rather than retaining it - was reported in a minority of the reviewed wetlands, and most of those had been created on former cropland or cattle pasture, where soil rich in phosphorus from its cropping history can release after construction (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_6); the rest were new wetlands released from initially phosphorus-rich sediments. That is the setting a rural scan targets, so legacy soil phosphorus belongs in the design brief. At site level a created basin exported total phosphorus in its tenth year while its twin barely retained any, after years of consistent retention (ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3), and sediment and total-phosphorus retention were diminishing after a decade of river flow (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5) - the sediment and phosphorus services age out while the nitrogen service holds. A substantial minority of individual wetlands showed no demonstrable nitrogen removal (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_8), and net annual release of nitrogen, though rare, has been observed (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_9). The quantified ceiling claims are modelled, not measured, and every unit is high-income temperate - inflows in the review included treated wastewater and urban runoff as well as agricultural runoff, so the pooled efficiency is not a farmland-only number.

wetland_management__establishment_cost.mechanism: The row rests on a measured construction cost from a large tropical peat rewetting trial: where dams are built in large volumes, the construction cost per compacted-peat canal dam is estimated at about 300 US$, which the authors describe as very economical compared with rewetting methods that use wood and other materials brought in from elsewhere [ev_project_cost_hooi24_4]. The mechanism behind the low cost is that the dam is built from the peat already on site, so the bill is machinery and labour rather than imported material and haulage.
wetland_management__establishment_cost.conditionality: The denominator is per structure, not per hectare, and it cannot be converted into a per-hectare establishment cost from this source: the number of dams a site needs depends on canal density and dam spacing, which the quoted passage does not give. No currency year is stated. This is a single trial in the Indonesian humid tropics on a retired pulpwood plantation, so it prices a specific rewetting technique in a specific peat landscape; it says nothing about the establishment cost of coastal, floodplain or inland wetland work, and nothing about land acquisition or compensation, which are excluded.

wetland_management__fire__all.mechanism: Rewetting drained peat — blocking canals so the water table rises — works on the fuel. Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland is stated to reduce fire risk through increased moisture in surface and below-ground fire fuels (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3), and improved hydrology after canal blocking is given as a route to reduced fire hazard (ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). Most of the cell describes the hazard from the loss side and the engine reads rewetting as the reversal of that chain: drainage and degradation made peat vulnerable to fire (ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1); cleared, drained and replanted peat domes become vulnerable to wildfires that, once started, can burn for years (ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1); the drier conditions following drainage increase the risk of fire (ev_wgy_ram_14); and in a hotter, drier European climate the risk of forest and peat fires in drained peatlands is expected to increase further (ev_wgy_qa_8). The one quantified result comes from a modelled fire-hazard index after large-scale canal-blocking rewetting in Riau, Sumatra: the frequency of continuous extreme-class hazard declined by 40% (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1).
wetland_management__fire__all.conditionality: The drainage-fire chain is asserted, not measured. The two newest statements come from advocacy-adjacent sources — a question-and-answer brief drafted for the EU Nature Restoration Law negotiations (ev_wgy_qa_8) and the Ramsar technical guidance on peatland rewetting (ev_wgy_ram_14) — and the others from an introductory book chapter (ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1) and a Ramsar briefing note (ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1); none measures fire before and after rewetting. The two restoration-frame claims are hedged as potential benefits, and Ritzema's is attributed to other studies rather than measured (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3, ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). The quantified study models hazard from weather data checked against satellite hotspots, not burned area, and its other results are weaker or opposite: the area under extreme-class hazard was only 5% lower after rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2); the mean duration of extreme events increased, with widespread prolonged extreme hazard occurring only in the drying El Niño years of 2015 and 2019 (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_3); and the authors conclude that duration was controlled by the weather and not influenced by rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_4). In the severe dry years, when the widespread prolonged extreme hazard occurred, no benefit is visible. The authors also caution that La Niña years drive part of the decline, so the rewetting effect may be overstated. Provenance: Indonesian and Malaysian humid-tropical peat in upper-middle-income settings, plus guidance statements with no site; nothing was measured in a low-income or lower-middle-income country, and the benefit lands on the landscape and on society, not on a farmer's plot.

wetland_management__fire__all__aez-humid.mechanism: In humid-tropical peat the lever is the water table. Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland raises moisture levels in surface and below-ground fire fuels (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3), and improved hydrology after canal blocking is the stated route to reduced fire hazard and to re-establishing forest vegetation (ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). The measured signal after canal-blocking rewetting is on event frequency: the frequency of continuous extreme-class fire hazard declined by 40% (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1).
wetland_management__fire__all__aez-humid.conditionality: The weaker signal in the same study is the area: mean area under extreme-class hazard was only 5% lower after rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2). Event duration rose rather than fell, with widespread prolonged extreme fire hazards occurring in drying El Niño years (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_3), and the authors' own reading is that duration was controlled by the weather and not influenced by rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_4). The supporting statements are hedged — potential benefits and a factor that could matter, not measured effects (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3, ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). Provenance: Indonesian and Malaysian peatland in upper-middle-income settings; humid-tropical peat elsewhere, and any low-income or lower-middle-income setting, is unrepresented, and the benefit is off the plot.

wetland_management__fire__all__income_gr.mechanism: Both units in this scope describe the mechanism from the loss side: peatland drainage and degradation are what made peat vulnerable to fire (ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1), and clearing, draining and replanting forested peat domes is what makes them vulnerable to wildfires that, once started, can burn for years (ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1). The implied practice effect is the reverse of that chain — restoring the water table re-wets the fuel — but neither unit measures it.
wetland_management__fire__all__income_gr.conditionality: Nothing in this scope is a measured restoration outcome. Both units are scene-setting statements, in an introductory book chapter and a policy brief, written in the loss frame and flipped by the engine into the restoration frame; neither carries a country, a region or a quantity. The pooled income context is mixed, so nothing in it is attached to a rural low-income or lower-middle-income landscape, and the benefit described accrues to the landscape and to society rather than on the farm. Any fire-risk claim for a specific site should be rebuilt from the measured rewetting evidence that sits in the wider fire cell, not from this scope.

wetland_management__fire__all__income_gr.mechanism: Rewetting raises the water table and with it the moisture of the fuel: restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland raises moisture levels in surface and below-ground fire fuels (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3), and improved hydrology after canal blocking is the stated route to reduced fire hazard (ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). The measured outcome after canal-blocking rewetting is a fall in event frequency: continuous extreme-class fire hazard declined by 40% (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1).
wetland_management__fire__all__income_gr.conditionality: The area signal in the same study is weak — mean area under extreme-class hazard only 5% lower after rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2) — and the duration signal runs against the benefit: mean duration of extreme events increased, with widespread prolonged extreme fire hazards occurring in drying El Niño years (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_3), while the authors attribute duration to weather rather than to rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_4). The two supporting claims are hedged rather than measured (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3, ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). Provenance: Indonesian and Malaysian humid-tropical peat only. An upper-middle-income peat landscape with industrial drainage canals is not a transferable analogue for a low-income smallholder wetland, and the fire-risk benefit accrues off the plot.

wetland_management__flood__all.mechanism: Flood peak and flood stage are different outcomes and this evidence moves them in different directions. Roughening and re-wetting the surface — re-vegetating bare peat, blocking gullies, lowering banks so water spreads onto a floodplain — slows storm-water delivery and cuts the discharge peak measured at or just below the works: 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N); 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); about 8% to 12% for a base-case modelled floodplain reconnection (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2). The loss frame agrees: bare peat gave higher peaks per unit rainfall (ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss) and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). Stage is the other half of the story — the same floodplain roughness that trims the downstream peak can double the size and depth of the inundated area for a flood of the same size (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up) — and timing is a third thing again: the gully whose peak fell by 49% also responded faster, its lag between rainfall and peak discharge shortening (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.
wetland_management__flood__all.conditionality: Catchment scale and extreme events are the unproven part. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment in the best-monitored UK test (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null); the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null); monitoring cannot isolate a restoration effect from catchment storm-flow data at all (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable); and the evidence does not suggest a major difference to downstream flood risk at large catchment scales, or for the most extreme events (ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null, ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null). During major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated and the presence, absence or management of wetlands has no effect (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null). The sign also flips with position: an on-site storage gain can still produce an increase in flood peaks at catchment scale through flood-wave synchrony (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff partially synchronised sub-catchment peaks and so increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); restoring the wrong reach worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects and in some scenarios raised aggregate flood damages above the no-restoration baseline (ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4); and moving the same project downstream along the channel turned a 14% peak reduction into about a 1% increase (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4). Rewetting also consumes flood storage: raising ditch water levels to meet winter ecological targets cost flood-water storage equivalent to 3% of the median annual flood volume (ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost) — the empty space a flood would fill is exactly what an ecological water-level target removes. Retention is a favourable-setting claim, not a general property: the Ramsar guidance says peatlands may, in favourable settings, function as retention areas after rewetting, especially where unused or used for paludiculture and so less vulnerable to inundation (ev_wgy_ram_13) — storage of flood water, which is a stage and volume service, not a general reduction of peaks. Provenance: this is a temperate, high-income corpus, UK and US catchments almost without exception, with no measured low-income or lower-middle-income result in scope; and the benefit is off the farm, arriving at downstream receptors rather than on the plot.

wetland_management__flood_hazard.mechanism: Flood peak and flood stage are different outcomes and this evidence moves them in different directions. Stage is the other half of the story — the same floodplain roughness that trims the downstream peak can double the size and depth of the inundated area for a flood of the same size (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up) — and timing is a third thing again: the gully whose peak fell by 49% also responded faster, its lag between rainfall and peak discharge shortening (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.

wetland_management__heat_stress_hazard.mechanism: Restored wetlands cool their surface by day by turning incoming energy into evaporation rather than sensible heat. On drained, subsided agricultural peat islands of the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, three wetlands constructed with managed water tables were significantly cooler by day than a drained alfalfa field on the same peat: up to 3.4 °C at the young wetland, 5.1 °C at the intermediate one and 2.1 °C at the oldest (ev_microclimate_buffering_hemes18_1). The comparator is the drained agricultural land the wetlands replaced, which is the right baseline for a decision to rewet farmland, rather than an intact reference wetland. The energy-balance contrast behind the cooling is illustrated from Trebon, Czech Republic: up to 60% to 70% of solar energy is transformed into sensible heat over a drained crop field against only 5% to 10% over an intact wetland, where 70% to 80% of heat is dissipated via evapotranspiration (ev_wet_microclimate_buffering_ramsar18_1).
wetland_management__heat_stress_hazard.conditionality: The cooling reverses twice, and both reversals are kept. The same wetlands were warmer than the alfalfa field through the night — up to 1.9 °C, 3.6 °C and 0.7 °C at the young, intermediate and old sites — as heat stored by day was released (ev_microclimate_buffering_hemes18_2); and at the seasonal scale a wetland was up to 2.3 °C warmer than alfalfa, mostly in spring and autumn, being cooler only at the height of the growing season (ev_microclimate_buffering_hemes18_3). The row's negative direction reflects these two reversal results; the daytime, growing-season cooling is the part that bears on daytime heat peaks, while the night-time warmth matters wherever night heat is the stress. All three Delta results are aerodynamic surface temperature, not air temperature, at one temperate delta, and none measures heat stress on people, crops or livestock nearby; the Trebon figures compare an intact wetland with a drained field, not a restored site. Provenance: two high-income temperate sources, the United States and the Czech Republic; no tropical, arid, low-income or lower-middle-income setting is represented, so neither the cooling nor its reversals can be assumed to carry over to the target contexts.

wetland_management__peatland__asset_thre.mechanism: Drought damages restored peat by dropping its water table. In a rewetted Indonesian peat restoration area, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). The authors read their long record as showing that a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface, with carbon-emission spikes, even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and remaining peat-swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6). The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to drought, as well as to fire, flooding and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_22).
wetland_management__peatland__asset_thre.conditionality: Only one unit is a measurement, from one Indonesian site; the second Hooijer unit is the authors' reading of their own record, and the Ramsar statement is expert knowledge with no frequency, site or measurement, made where the guidance itself notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. The cell is humid-tropical peat in an upper-middle-income setting; no temperate peat and no low-income or lower-middle-income site is represented. Design implication: a rewetting investment in drought-prone tropical peat should expect the asset to lose surface elevation and carbon, and plantings to fail, in El Niño years however well the water management performs, and should budget and monitor for that rather than treat it as a failure of the works.

wetland_management__peatland__biodiversi.mechanism: Raising the water table and removing the degrading pressure is what allows peatland vegetation to re-establish, and adding an active revegetation step is what makes it quick. Enhanced restoration using moss-layer transfer brought Sphagnum cover towards, and potentially past, intact levels and reached intact-level specialist plant diversity within years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_7); basic rewetting and tree felling produced marked recovery on a multi-decadal path (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_2); and the systematic review's own summary is that active restoration or replacement measures are needed to speed recolonisation of bare peat (ev_biodiversity_outcome_rasa23_10). In Belarus, vegetation mapping after rewetting 950 ha of the Dokudovskoe cut-over peatland found Phragmites-sedge communities on at least 398 ha, against no more than 20 ha at baseline (ev_wgy_blr_7). Where only the upper peat layer had been removed, biological structure recovered immediately (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_10). On tropical peat the same lever appears as native peat-swamp-forest trees regrowing spontaneously in the most rewetted conditions (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
wetland_management__peatland__biodiversi.conditionality: Structure returning is not function returning, and neither is the same as matching an intact site. In restored peatlands, Sphagnum cover and peatland specialist cover remained well below intact peatlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_1), and where biological structure did recover immediately the biogeochemical functioning of the same peatlands stayed statistically below reference decades later (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_10) - so a row that reads as a biodiversity gain against a degraded baseline still carries a shortfall against the intact reference, and the comparisons must not be netted against each other. The restoration method decides whether there is any result at all within an investment horizon: passive restoration was projected over centuries (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5), with specialist cover stagnating or further deteriorating long after abandonment (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6), and stressor removal without revegetation appeared to cause a decline in specialist diversity, a response the authors could not predict reliably (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_8). The Belarus result shows the same dependence on active work: it fell short of the target of at least 700 ha, sedge seed was practically absent from the donor bogs for three years so only 70 ha were planted or sown, and reed and cattail were first to appear on the rest, expected to give way to sedge as the sites develop (ev_wgy_blr_7). The temperate and boreal evidence is substantial and mostly high-income; the tropical units are thin, bundled with clearing and seed proximity, and partly a stated potential rather than a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4), so transferring this row to a tropical peat landscape rests on mechanism, not on matched evidence.

wetland_management__peatland__carbon_seq.mechanism: On peat, the units that weigh all the gases together set the direction, and where they state a horizon they favour rewetting over the drained state, along a time path. On a hundred-year global warming potential basis, rewetting drained organic soils gives net annual removals of carbon dioxide in most soil classes, an increase in annual methane, a decrease in nitrous oxide and dissolved organic carbon, and a lowering of net greenhouse-gas emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_4]; every 10 cm the effective water-table depth is raised cuts the net warming of carbon dioxide plus methane by at least 3 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 until the table is within 30 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1], and between 5 and 13 cm depth the carbon dioxide cooling exceeds the methane warming [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_5]. Other sources refuse a fixed horizon and report radiative forcing through time, finding that it plateaus soon after rewetting because carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide stop while the methane is short-lived, so the methane forcing does not undermine the mitigation and the carbon dioxide cost of delay is much higher [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_5]. The question-and-answer document on peatland rewetting, citing the literature, states that rewetting initially causes a slight warming impact because of increased methane, but that in the longer term the result is cooling [ev_wgy_qa_3, ev_wgy_qa_4]; the Ramsar technical report, also citing studies, holds that the combined fluxes of carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and dissolved organic carbon are very positive for the climate compared with the former drained situation [ev_wgy_ram_1], and that even after a disproportionally large initial methane peak the longer-term effects are much better than maintaining the drained status quo [ev_wgy_ram_3]. A German study cited in a Scottish evidence assessment found 17 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 saved by rewetting a reed-canary-grass peatland compared with its drained state [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_1]. The size of the prize is set by what drainage is already costing. Water-table decline stimulates heterotrophic rather than autotrophic soil respiration and raises the subsidence rate across climate zones and land uses [ev_wetflA_ma_wt_respiration]; drained peatlands release 645 Mt C yr-1 through soil respiration, about 5% of global annual anthropogenic carbon emissions [ev_wetflA_ma_global_release], the per-hectare losses highest in the drained tropics at 10,865 to 23,685 kg C ha-1 yr-1 [ev_wetflA_ma_tropical_rates]; degraded peat emits 2 Gt CO2 a year, nearly a quarter of land-sector emissions and up more than 25% since 1990 [ev_carbon_sequestration_bonn16_2]; and tropical peat drained for plantation lost an average 100 t CO2eq ha-1 yr-1 over 25 yr, 178 in the first 5 yr [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_2]. Rewetting reverses the aerobic decomposition but re-establishes methane, and both gases have to be named [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1]. Both advocacy-adjacent documents assert the same exchange: rewetting stops carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide but re-installs methane [ev_wgy_qa_1, ev_wgy_qa_2, ev_wgy_ram_2]; and while the table stays below the surface, peat-oxidation emissions fall roughly linearly as it is raised, so roughly half can be avoided by raising it to half its former depth — the oxidation term only [ev_wgy_ram_4]. The peatland subgroup of a restoration meta-analysis shows the same shape, with significant increases in above- and belowground biomass and soil carbon and significant carbon dioxide flux reductions [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_7]. In the tropics the measured route is subsidence: canal blocking halved it where water tables rose from about -0.6 m to about -0.3 m [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2], implying a carbon emission reduction of 6.4 to 23.6 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in the well-rewetted area [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1], and dams can permanently raise the water table in a degraded peat dome, which reduces subsidence and carbon dioxide emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_1].
wetland_management__peatland__carbon_seq.conditionality: What the peat was drained for decides the net result. The Ramsar report, citing studies, states that rewetting tropical peat and agricultural peat outside the tropics always has a large and rapid mitigation effect, while on boreal forestry-drained peat the effect may be much lower and slower, complicated by albedo change and by carbon dioxide emissions after clear-cutting [ev_wgy_ram_5], in line with the forestry-drained results below. On tropical cropland and plantation peat, rewetting caused an immediate, almost linearly increasing cooling, the rising methane offsetting only a few per cent of the cooling from falling carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3]. On temperate and boreal agricultural peat the methane warming offsets a major part of that cooling for the first decades [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_4]. On forestry-drained peat the increased methane offsets over 100% of the cooling for at least the first 40 years and still at least 50% a century later, so rewetting there warms over the policy-relevant horizon, and it also decreases the carbon stored in the trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_1]. Water above the peat surface is the other reversal: raising average water levels above the surface is likely to make the methane warming exceed the carbon dioxide cooling over shorter horizons [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]; taking the table from 30 cm depth to the surface adds about 7 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 of methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_2], where stopping at 30 cm has a negligible effect, at most 0.3 [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_3]; and moderate rewetting to 10-20 cm below the surface prevents a major portion of peat loss without causing high methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_6]. Paludiculture and permanence add reversals: the 25-30 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 reduction quoted for paludiculture is mostly avoided emissions from deep-drained cropland, and field experiments disagree on whether such sites become a net carbon dioxide sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_2]; harvesting Sphagnum biomass is judged likely to prevent the peat from being a long-term carbon store and to cause further degradation, a review judgement rather than a measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_3]; and converting rewetted peat back to agriculture is estimated to release 6.5 t C ha-1 yr-1, a carbon-only loss figure [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_4]. The remaining reversals are kept rather than averaged away: higher emissions were estimated from rewetted temperate nutrient-rich forest sites than from their drained counterparts [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_5]; a rewetted Irish peatland emitted more methane than natural sites and its global warming potential was still above intact peatland after a decade, even though its carbon dioxide emission factor had fallen significantly to 104 g CO2-C m-2 yr-1 [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]; a fertilised reed-canary-grass plot on cutover peat emitted 21,938 kg CO2 ha-1 yr-1 against 8,448 from the natural bog, although the same plots emitted far less methane than the bog and had lower global warming potential than bare peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_5]; an upland English rewetting raised methane significantly in the sparsely vegetated pans while photosynthesis and ecosystem respiration did not move, so nothing on the carbon dioxide side offset it [ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up, ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null]; cutaway-peat restoration cut soil carbon dioxide emission and raised methane together, and after a decade some restored sites still showed a more warming balance and higher sensitivity to climate anomalies than intact peatland [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_3]; a methane peak in the first years after rewetting has been reported [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_6]; and the peatland subgroup records methane rising significantly alongside its carbon dioxide and stock benefits [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_8]. Much of the apparent disagreement here is between gases rather than between findings: single-gas units are parts of the ledger, so a carbon dioxide fall and a methane rise taken from the same sentence enter with opposite signs [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_2]; and the one recovery-shortfall unit says peatland biogeochemical function remained statistically lower than reference wetlands 30 y after restoration, which is a statement about rebuilding an intact peatland, not about losing carbon against the drained baseline [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_11]. Programme totals and single-gas figures cannot carry a net claim: the Belarus terminal evaluation's per-hectare estimates of 7.1 tons per year after rewetting and 4.9 after 20 years, reported as a 65 % reduction with 75 % anticipated after 20 years, are carbon dioxide only with no methane reported, and modelled [ev_wgy_blr_3, ev_wgy_blr_4]; Indonesia's Peatland Restoration Agency attributes approximately 285 million tons of CO2eq of reduction to water management on the strength of a water-level monitoring database, not measured fluxes [ev_carbon_sequestration_cifor270_1]. The tropical evidence is the thinnest and the most investable. The tropical rewetting scenarios rest on default emission factors [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3], and the source of those factors states plainly that no studies exist on rewetted tropical sites with the water table close to the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1]; the tropical rows of the water-table synthesis are extrapolated from temperate and boreal relationships rather than measured [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_6]. Measured tropical results are muted: a year after canal damming in Central Kalimantan, carbon dioxide emissions were 7305 then 7444 g m-2 yr-1 at the forest site and 2781 then 2608 at the deforested burned site, read by the authors as no marked response [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2]; the deforested site stayed a weak methane source and the source grew [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3] while the forest floor stayed a weak sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4]; higher water tables had a relatively small effect on annual methane budgets [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5]; raising the groundwater level hardly reduces peat-surface carbon dioxide flux in drained forest, because root respiration dominates it [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_2]; regrowth on open restored areas is still too small to compensate peat decomposition [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_3]; the higher water tables did not completely compensate the increased subsidence near the canals [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_5]; canal blocking is a long-term measure that works through vegetation regeneration rather than on its own [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_6]; inside a drained plantation that stays in production the ceiling is a reduction of no more than 20% [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1]; and the Southeast Asian reviews call the outcomes inconclusive, with decomposition continuing in the saturated zone and carbon leaving as methane or through fluvial networks, so a rewetted peatland cannot be expected to behave like a natural one in its gas exchange [ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_2]. The remaining tropical claim is a direction-only review line about a bundled rewetting and fire-prevention programme, with no magnitude and no comparator [ev_carbon_sequestration_alex26_2], beside general statements of potential [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_erwi09_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_9].

wetland_management__peatland__cost_per_h.mechanism: Peatland rewetting by blocking drainage canals is a low-engineering intervention spread over very large areas, which keeps the per-hectare cost in the low thousands of US dollars: Indonesia's national rewetting programme is estimated at US$2,300/ha, with planning and construction in Germany at €2,363/ha [ev_wgy_ram_19], and a national review cites an average of around USD1,866 ha-1 within a total of USD1.7 to 7 billion [ev_project_cost_alex26_1].
wetland_management__peatland__cost_per_h.conditionality: Both Indonesian figures are programme-level estimates cited second-hand, with no price year, no split between rewetting, revegetation and revitalisation, and (for the national total) no stated area denominator. They come from an upper-middle-income country; no low-income peatland cost is in the pool. Use them as an order of magnitude, not a budget line.

wetland_management__peatland__cost_reduc.mechanism: Farming a rewetted peatland costs more than farming it drained: wet cultivation brings higher risk, high investment costs and the need for specialised harvesting equipment and adapted production [ev_wet_cost_neud26_3]. At the high-input extreme, establishing a Sphagnum production field on former bog grassland, calculated from pilot cost data in 2011 and 2016, cost in the order of a hundred thousand euros per hectare, lower at the later date [ev_wgy_wich_7].
wetland_management__peatland__cost_reduc.conditionality: European evidence only (German pilot plus a scoping review whose economics corpus is mostly European). The Sphagnum figures describe topsoil removal, pumped irrigation and specialised machinery, far beyond simple ditch blocking; low-input rewetting would cost far less, but no source here quantifies it.

wetland_management__peatland__flood__all.mechanism: Re-vegetating bare peat and blocking grips and gullies raises surface roughness and storage on the hillslope, so storm water is delivered more slowly. Peak discharge fell 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, both against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N), and 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); lag between peak rainfall and peak flow lengthened significantly at the re-vegetated site (ev_wetflA_shut_lag_O), restoration elsewhere produced lower discharge rates observable at drain and hill-stream level, with greater water-table stability and a reduction in peak flows (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_field), and modelling suggests drain blocking in blanket peat could reduce flood flows downstream (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_model). The loss frame points the same way: higher flood peaks and shorter times to peak go with peatland degradation and removal of vegetation cover (ev_wetflA_dads_degradation_loss, ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss). Peak and timing do not behave alike as storms grow — at the gully-blocked site the peak reduction held at 56% in the largest storms while the lag gain collapsed (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_largestorm_N, ev_wetflA_shut_lag_largestorm_N) — and at the rewetted gully the lag shortened even as the peak fell (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). Restoration changed the timing and the peak of delivery but not the volume: the runoff coefficient was unchanged at both restored sites (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.
wetland_management__peatland__flood__all.conditionality: The measurements are plot to micro-catchment; the catchment-scale benefit is not demonstrated. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null), the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null), the monitoring authors state that isolating restoration effects within empirical storm-flow datasets is problematic at the large catchment scale (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable), and a realistic suite of land-management changes modelled against an extreme rainfall event gave a median flood-peak reduction of only 2% (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_model_2pct). Position decides the sign: upland wetlands tend to be flood-generating areas, frequently saturated with little water storage potential (ev_wetflA_acre_position_upland); blanket bogs close to saturation for most of the year rarely attenuate flow and are much more likely to contribute to storm runoff (ev_wetflA_acre_saturated_bog_reversal); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff synchronised sub-catchment peaks and increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); and an on-site storage gain can still raise peaks at catchment scale (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment). Even on the hillslope the lever is conditional: ditch blocking in upland peat reduces flow peaks only in the steepest, smoothest drains, with the roughness of the surrounding vegetated peat mattering more than the ditches (ev_wetflA_dads_ditchblock_conditional), and upland ditches may increase or decrease local flood peaks depending on layout, topography and synchronisation (ev_wetflA_dads_ditch_sign_flip). The review covering this family reports moderate flood-reduction results but without empirical evidence for larger-scale effects (ev_wetflA_zhu_peatland_confidence). Retention is a favourable-setting claim, not a general property: the Ramsar guidance says peatlands may, in favourable settings, function as retention areas after rewetting, especially where unused or used for paludiculture and so less vulnerable to inundation (ev_wgy_ram_13) — storage of flood water, which is a stage and volume service, not a general reduction of peaks. The state-dependence statements (ev_wgy_ram_10, ev_wgy_ram_11, ev_wgy_ram_12) are guidance-level synthesis, two with their own references and one an expert assertion; they establish that the sign depends on the peat's starting state, on top of its catchment position, but not how often each case occurs. Provenance: UK blanket peat carries almost the whole cell, with a Chinese high-altitude degradation case and a Newfoundland bog; it is temperate and high-income, with no low-income or lower-middle-income measurement, and the benefit arrives downstream rather than on the plot.
