wetland_management__peatland__production.mechanism: There are two horizons. In the short term, rewetting ends drainage-based cropping: food crops such as potatoes and carrots become unsuitable [ev_wgy_qa_6], high and low water-table uses cannot share a peatland [ev_wgy_ram_17], and paludicrops are mostly non-edible [ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]; Finland reports a minor national but a local effect [ev_wgy_qa_5]. In the long term, keeping peat drained also loses production: subsidence on deep SE Asian peat may cause loss of agricultural production once gravity drainage fails [ev_agricultural_production_value_hooi12_3], and the drained Mega Rice Project land proved largely unsuitable for rice, threatening local livelihoods [ev_agricultural_production_value_ritz13_9].
wetland_management__peatland__production.conditionality: The class and its evidence disagree in kind. The positive direction comes from studies of draining tropical peat (oil palm, Acacia, the Mega Rice Project), which document the cost of keeping peat drained, not a measured yield after rewetting; it is an avoided-future-loss argument. The measured-style evidence on rewetting itself, all European, points to a near-term production loss. No low-income source. Treat as: rewetting costs production now and may avoid larger losses later on deep, subsiding tropical peat.

wetland_management__peatland__rural_pove.mechanism: On rewetted peat, household income depends on finding a product that sells. Across countries, paludiculture is generally not profitable at farm level when revenue relies solely on biomass sales [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1], income is hard to keep at the conventional level [ev_wet_econret_temm26_4], and SE Asian oil palm communities face lower returns under rewetting [ev_household_income_mish21_5]. Harvesting existing reed stands shows the spread: thatching bundles have a mode of € 572 ha-1 a-1 with a risk of loss below 1 % [ev_wgy_wich_1], combustion bales a mode of € 53 with an 18 % risk of loss [ev_wgy_wich_2], and biogas chaff a loss in the mode (€ 195 ha-1 a-1) with a 98 % risk of loss because demand and price are low [ev_wgy_wich_3]. Farmed Sphagnum is profitable as founder material even in the most pessimistic scenario [ev_wgy_wich_6] but cannot compete with peat as growing media [ev_wgy_wich_4].
wetland_management__peatland__rural_pove.conditionality: The class and its evidence disagree. The slight positive rests on reed figures from existing reed beds, not fields created by rewetting drained land [ev_wgy_wich_1, ev_wgy_wich_2]; on niche Sphagnum markets; on an asserted SDG mapping that holds only 'if available' payments exist [ev_wet_hhinc_temm26_6]; on a society-level benefit-cost estimate for the EU [ev_wgy_qa_7]; and on an editorial claim about Chinese peatlands [ev_rural_poverty_bonn16_3]. The pooled review conclusion is that mainstream paludiculture does not pay. Belarus found no direct household benefit because none was designed [ev_wgy_blr_1]. No low-income evidence; for a low-income peatland, expect a household cost unless payments or a high-value product are built in.

wetland_management__peatland__soil_erosi.mechanism: Re-vegetating bare blanket peat and blocking gullies with stone and timber dams puts a plant cover and physical barriers between rainfall and exposed peat, which is the route by which peatland restoration would reduce sediment loss. On the quantity measured here - the share of storm rainfall leaving as storm discharge - restoration changed nothing at either restored site relative to the bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null). The Ramsar technical report, citing the literature, states that disturbed peatlands release substantial quantities of suspended solids and that drain-blocking generally leads to a substantial reduction in their outflow (ev_wgy_ram_7).
wetland_management__peatland__soil_erosi.conditionality: The no-effect reading is about water volume, not soil. The single unit behind this row is a runoff-coefficient null (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null), and the paper's own conclusion is that restoration altered the timing and peak of storm delivery while leaving the volume of runoff produced unchanged. It is therefore evidence that re-vegetation and gully blocking did not reduce how much water ran off, and it should not be read as evidence that they fail to reduce erosion - no sediment or soil-loss measurement is present in this pool. The only sediment statement is the Ramsar report's cited synthesis on suspended-solid outflow, which gives no magnitude and no site (ev_wgy_ram_7). The measured observation is a single upland English blanket-peat site in a high-income temperate setting, with no tropical peat and no farmland, so this row marks an evidence gap rather than a finding of no effect.

wetland_management__peatland__water_qual.mechanism: Rewetting a cut-over peat site - raising the water table, filling or blocking ditches, mulching and transferring a moss layer - stabilises the water table and keeps the exposed peat saturated, so less nutrient and carbon load is flushed from the surface. Against the realistic do-nothing counterfactual of an abandoned extraction site, the loads leaving restored sites were lower (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). The Ramsar technical report, citing the literature, generalises this: disturbed peatlands release substantial quantities of humic acids, nitrogen, sulphur, heavy metals and suspended solids, whereas drain-blocking generally leads to a substantial reduction in their outflow (ev_wgy_ram_6, ev_wgy_ram_7).
wetland_management__peatland__water_qual.conditionality: The gain is measured against the degraded starting point, and against that baseline restored extraction sites leak less (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). Measured against their intact natural counterparts the same restored sites leaked more nutrients and carbon, associated with greater water-table variation (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_4); that is incomplete recovery towards an intact peatland, not harm, and the two comparisons must not be netted. The real reversals are in the Ramsar report's cited synthesis. In some cases restoration causes a temporarily increased flush of nutrients into downstream water courses, though the release decreases in the longer term (ev_wgy_ram_8); and on nutrient-rich, formerly fertilised agricultural fens, rewetting may even increase the nutrient problem by mobilising hitherto bound phosphorus and nitrogen, internal eutrophication (ev_wgy_ram_9). Agricultural peat is exactly the land a rural scan would target, so a downstream nutrient pulse in the early years, and a sustained phosphorus problem on fertilised fens, should be planned for rather than assumed away. The measured case in this pool found no significant water-quality improvement and no significant reduction in aqueous carbon losses after rewetting an eroding upland blanket peat, with dissolved organic carbon rising non-significantly afterwards (ev_wetflA_gatis_waterquality_null); the quantity measured there is dissolved organic carbon routed to the nearest water-quality outcome, not nutrients, and water colour did change. Everything here is boreal or temperate peat in high-income countries or unspecified settings; nothing covers tropical peat or a farmed low- or lower-middle-income catchment, and the Ramsar statements give direction without magnitude or site.

wetland_management__peatland__water_stre.mechanism: On peat, rewetting puts the water table back towards where the drain took it from. Across boreo-temperate wetlands, the effects of peatland restoration and drainage were of similar magnitude but opposite direction, so on average rewetting a drained peatland can be expected to restore groundwater levels near the ditch [ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. On an eroding English upland peatland, peat barriers built across gullies raised mean water tables significantly at every distance class, in the peat pans from 0.003 m below ground level to 0.064 m above it and in the vegetated haggs from 0.188 to 0.175 m below ground within 0.5 m of the pan edge [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. On cutaway peat, the water-table level was successfully recovered by active restoration through ditch blocking and dam construction [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_6].
wetland_management__peatland__water_stre.conditionality: Restoration may not reach all the area that drainage affected, and the outcome depends strongly on local context [ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. The English rise is in the mean rather than the typical state: median water-table conditions remained similar at all distances after restoration, so the significant mean rise is driven by the wet tail [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. Water-table fluctuation and the moisture dynamics of the peat layer were found difficult to maintain in restored peat-extraction areas, so the level returns but its dynamics do not [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7]; and many hydrological processes do not fully recover within the first years after restoration, because degradation has already changed peat structure and consolidation, so early results are not the steady state and the monitoring windows behind most restoration claims are shorter than the recovery time [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]. Every unit is temperate or boreal, from the UK, Ireland, Canada, Fennoscandia and northern Europe; none is from a low- or lower-middle-income setting, and none measures water available to a farming system or water stress experienced by farmers.

wetland_management__production_gap.mechanism: Restoration widens the gap where the restored land was itself farmed or where wildlife from the restored wetland reaches neighbouring fields. Rewetted peat becomes unsuitable for crops such as potatoes and carrots [ev_wgy_qa_6], drainage-based agriculture cannot be combined with high water tables in the same peatland [ev_wgy_ram_17], and paludicrops are mostly non-edible, so the transition can mean a local net loss of food production [ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]. Near the protected Poyang Lake wetland, tenant farmers' crops are damaged by migratory birds and other wild animals with no compensation [ev_wgy_poy_2]. Against this, in Uganda the matched GCF evaluation found the aggregate yield effect positive but not statistically significant [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5], and in Ghana clearing a 7 km creek to the Songor lagoon enhanced cattle farming along it [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2].
wetland_management__production_gap.conditionality: The loss is local, not national: a Finnish study found only minor impact on national food production but local challenges in peatland-rich municipalities [ev_wgy_qa_5]. Most of the negative evidence is expert assertion from European peatland policy briefs; the only matched counterfactual in a low-income country shows no yield change either way. Expect a production cost where restoration converts farmed land (drained peat, reclaimed lakebed); expect little change where it restores already-degraded, uncultivated wetland.

wetland_management__production_gap__inco.mechanism: In high-income peatland regions the gap opens because rewetting replaces drainage-based food crops with mostly non-edible paludicrops, which can mean a local or regional net loss of food production [ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]. Nationally the effect can be small: in Finland, rewetting agriculturally used peatlands had only minor impact on food production and food security, with challenges concentrated in peatland-rich municipalities [ev_wgy_qa_5].
wetland_management__production_gap__inco.conditionality: Both sources are European review or policy-brief statements, not measured farm outcomes, and neither gives a size. The loss falls on the farms and municipalities whose land is rewetted, not on national supply; scoping should look for concentration of drained peat in a few districts.

wetland_management__production_gap__inco.mechanism: In low-income settings the evidence is thin and points both ways. The Uganda GCF evaluation, a matched comparison, found that a broader crop portfolio around restored wetlands gave a positive but not statistically significant change in aggregate yield [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5]. In Ghana, a community cleared a 7 km creek reconnecting the Volta River to the Songor lagoon, which interviewees said increased fish yields and enhanced cattle farming along the creek [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2].
wetland_management__production_gap__inco.conditionality: The class and its strongest evidence disagree. The slight positive rests on a single village account from an evaluation interview in Ghana; the matched household study in Uganda finds no significant yield effect. Read this row as no demonstrated change in production for low-income restoration, with a possible gain where reconnection restores water to grazing land.

wetland_management__recurrent_cost.mechanism: The recurring cost of wetland restoration in this US national model is the land payment that covers the opportunity cost of land taken out of agricultural production: land rental costs for cropland are, in the mean, more than five times greater than those for pastureland, at US$274 ± 156 per hectare [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6]. Design, construction and maintenance enter the same framework as area-dependent costs, annualised over a 50-year management horizon at a real discount rate of 4%, with the rental rates taken from state-level agricultural statistics.
wetland_management__recurrent_cost.conditionality: This is a modelled national cost framework, and the dominant recurrent item is a US cropland rental rate, which prices forgone agriculture in a high-income economy — it cannot be read across to a low- or lower-middle-income landscape, where the opportunity cost of farmland is set by quite different land and tenure arrangements. No currency year is stated in the quoted passage. The denominator is per hectare per year and should be kept that way: it is not an establishment cost, and it must not be rolled together with the per-hectare project totals elsewhere in this bundle. The useful general point is structural rather than numerical — where wetlands are restored on farmland, the standing cost is the production forgone, not the maintenance of the works.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Drought can switch off the flood pulse a restored floodplain depends on. On a restored floodplain the hazard works by removing the flood the wetland depends on: in 2020, lack of snow cover and severe drought meant no spring flooding on the Pripyat floodplain, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly (ev_wgy_blr_6).
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: This is one observation in a project terminal evaluation from Belarus, an upper-middle-income temperate setting, and the practice is restoration and maintenance of open floodplain meadows by grazing and mowing, not rewetting of drained land; the indicator is the number of migrating and nesting birds, not a livelihood or a hydrological measure, and the evaluation gives no size for the decline. It also names drought and snowless winters as arriving faster and more severely than the project was designed for. The lesson that transfers is a design one: a floodplain wetland fed by a seasonal flood is exposed whenever drought removes that flood, so its habitat function, and anything that depends on it, should be expected to fail in such years.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Reinstating hydrology on a degraded wetland puts back standing water and saturated soil, and the gain is measured against that degraded starting point. Restoring degraded wetlands enhanced biodiversity overall and the diversity of vertebrates, vascular plants and terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3). The mobile parts of the system return first: vertebrate assemblages reached reference structural values within a few years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6), and riverine and tidal wetlands kept connected by natural flow variation recovered biological structure and biogeochemical function within a couple of decades (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9). Project cases show the same fast early response. After the first test flooding of the restored Belene Island marshes, park reports cited by the World Bank record fish species rising from 2 to 10 within 2 months and ferruginous duck nesting pairs from 5 to 50 (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1); a project-supported inventory found flora and fauna beginning to regenerate after the Lapusna wetland in Moldova was restored (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). Two units come from protecting existing wetlands rather than restoring them: in Lao PDR, designating fishery conservation zones was followed by an increase in native fish populations and more fish for local consumption (ev_wgy_lao_3), and at Sierra Leone's Mamunta Mayosso sanctuary positive changes in biodiversity conservation are confirmed after cattle settlements were banned (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1).
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: A restored wetland that falls short of an intact one is a recovery note, not harm, and it is kept apart from the gain above. The slow parts lag: plant assemblages took decades to converge statistically with reference sites and their absolute structural values remained below reference a century after restoration, with biological structure and biogeochemical functioning still lower than reference (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1), while inland depressional wetlands fed only by precipitation or groundwater had not recovered to reference conditions decades after restoration (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8). The two global syntheses disagree on whether that shortfall persists, since biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2). Not every group responds: macroinvertebrate diversity showed no significant effect (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4). The project units are weaker than their numbers suggest. The Bulgarian counts are park reports taken within months of the first flooding (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2), and the Moldovan result is direction only (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). The Sierra Leone claim is an evaluator's assertion about a bundle of grazing by-laws, boundary demarcation and co-management, and it depended on the exit of all Fula settlements and their cattle, a livelihood cost the biodiversity gain does not show (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1). The Lao result rests on project fish-monitoring records inside protected zones (ev_wgy_lao_3). The Ugandan Green Climate Fund baseline found few significant differences in phytoplankton, green algae, flagellates, zooplankton and crustaceans between treatment and comparison wetland systems; it is a baseline for a restoration bundled with access restrictions and livelihood support, not an impact estimate (ev_biodiversity_outcome_fp034b_1).

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: The net balance comes first. Rewetting degraded wetlands at rates matching historical degradation cuts greenhouse-gas emissions by 583.8 to 782 t CO2eq ha-1 under its two scenarios [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_1], of which carbon dioxide alone carries 77.6% in the all-rewetting case [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_2], and the radiative forcing caused by methane and nitrous oxide is fully compensated by carbon dioxide uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_3] — a volume equivalent to ten percent of anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_7]. The design target follows from the water-table gradient: the sum of all three gases is lowest, near zero, when the water table is near the ground surface, between -30 and -5 cm [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_4], against 19.7 and 11.2 t CO2eq ha-1 yr-1 from boreal and temperate wetlands held at or below -70 cm [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_6]. Measurements over a mesonetwork of restored wetlands on drained Californian peat showed that conversion can, in some cases, yield a net greenhouse-gas benefit compared with the original land use [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_5]. Behind that balance sit the parts of the ledger. Pooled across restored and altered wetlands, carbon dioxide flux fell significantly (SMD -0.43; CI -0.84 to -0.01; k = 111) [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_1], soil carbon rose (SMD 0.62; CI 0.23 to 0.99; k = 207) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cama26_4], and aboveground and belowground biomass rose by the largest effect sizes in the analysis (SMD 2.52 and 1.94) [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_6], while nitrous oxide showed a non-significant trend towards reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_3]. Restoring degraded hydric soils is held to have a high potential for sequestrating soil carbon, because flooding restores the anoxic conditions optimal for accretion of organic matter [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: Two distinct things pull this row negative, and neither is a finding that rewetting releases more carbon than leaving the peat drained. The first is methane, a single-gas part of the ledger rather than a net balance: methane flux rose after restoration (SMD 0.44; CI 0.14 to 0.74; k = 95) [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_2], hydrological interventions specifically produced elevated methane alongside reduced nitrous oxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_9], methane is maximal where water levels stand well above the soil surface and minimal where the table is well below it [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_5], and carbon dioxide emissions decline soon after restoration while methane typically rises in the short term, with emerging evidence that the rise weakens as the ecosystem matures [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_11]; restored freshwater marshes accrete soil carbon at the cost of significant methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_4], and the same source's net statement holds only in some cases [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_5]. Those are the methane halves of the very sentences whose carbon dioxide halves sit in the mechanism above, and the same sources conclude a net benefit [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_3]. The second is the comparator: units measuring restored wetlands against intact reference wetlands rather than against the degraded baseline — soil carbon still 50% lower after 20 y [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_2], organic matter at 62% of reference at 20-30 y [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_3], biogeochemical function at 79% of reference at 30 y in temperate and 53% at 50 y in cold climates [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_13, ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_12], and climate regulation the largest service shortfall against natural wetlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_meli14_6]. Read together, the pool says rewetting cuts the net balance while raising methane, and that a rewetted site stays below an intact one for decades. Real limits remain. The near-zero optimum and the methane gradient are read across the water tables of existing wetlands rather than before and after at rewetted sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_6]. The meta-analysis is a preprint whose tropical and arid pairs are under-represented, with publication bias detected for the stock terms, so those effect sizes are likely inflated [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cama26_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_6]. The global scenarios are modelled projections, and no horizon is stated for the per-hectare figure [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_7]. The supporting gain statements are assertions of potential with no rate, country or climate zone attached [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3]. Nothing in this scope row is a measurement at a rewetted tropical site, and the prior land use that the tropical case turns on is not distinguished anywhere in this pool.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Reconnecting floodplains costs what the water-control works and land access cost: in Bulgaria, building infrastructure to allow controlled flooding of former Danube marshes cost US$1,903/ha at completion [ev_project_cost_bgieg_1]; in Vermont, wetland revegetation of disconnected reaches is costed at $3200 ha-1 for labour and materials [ev_project_cost_gour20_5].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: Both sources are high-income and neither states a currency year. The Bulgarian figure divides total project cost (including protected-area management) by restored area; the Vermont figure is a model input that leaves out the land easement, which the paper costs separately. Out of context for low-income targets; no local cost evidence for this family.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Wetlands hold water through the wet season and release it slowly, so they can keep a river flowing when the rain stops. In a distributed hydrological model of the Nenjiang basin, riparian wetlands overall alleviated drought [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2], and across most of the modelled scenarios the loss of minimum flow and the rise in drought deficit caused by removing wetlands outweighed the gains, meaning the wetlands overall supported low flow during the severe drought of 2011 [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The sign depends on the type and position of the wetland: in the same model, isolated wetlands could intensify the drought deficit to some extent, because water stored away from the channel evaporates instead of sustaining low flow [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_3]. Every unit behind this row comes from a single modelling study in temperate northeast China, and the model works by removing wetlands that already exist rather than by restoring any, so it is evidence for keeping wetlands more than for rebuilding them [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2, ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6]. Nothing was measured in the field, no magnitude is attached to the drought relief, and no claim is made about a farm: the water arrives downstream.

All of the evidence is a single modelling study in temperate, upper-middle-income northeast China, and it works by deleting wetlands that already exist from the model rather than by restoring any, so it supports conserving wetlands more directly than building them [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2, ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6]. wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Reconnecting and rewetting floodplain and depressional wetland puts storm water somewhere other than the channel. Modelled peak flow fell by up to 37% at the reach scale, and by up to 19% where banks were lowered furthest (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_1, ev_flood_hazard_feder22_6); wooded wetlands increase flood storage, reduce flood peaks and increase peak travel time (ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland); depressional wetlands could store 72% of the total runoff volume of a 2-year rainfall event (ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage); and in the loss frame, embanking a floodplain to remove its storage raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). Peak and stage are separate outcomes that move apart: removing the levees lowered cross-sectional water-surface elevation by an average of 0.66 m (ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_1) while decreasing peak discharge over the same segment by less than 0.04 to 0.13% (ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_3), and roughening the floodplain with shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for the same flood (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up).
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The clear evidence is explicitly local and explicitly for moderate rainfall events (ev_wetflA_dads_summary_moderate); for the most extreme events, and at large catchment scales, the evidence does not suggest a major effect on downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null, ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null), during major catastrophic floods the presence or absence of wetlands has no effect (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null), and the storable share of a flood falls with rarity — the same depressional wetlands held 72% of the runoff volume of a 2-year event but 41% of a 100-year event (ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage). At the catchment outlet the modelled changes are small: 0.65% off the Q100 peak, 1.1% off the Q25 peak, and no change in flood volume for the Q2 storm (ev_flood_hazard_worl23_2, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_3, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_4), with only modest peak attenuation across the design storms because of the steep, flashy setting (ev_flood_hazard_worl23_1); and the aggregated effects of multiple wetlands can differ considerably from the functions observed at individual wetland scale (ev_wetflA_thor_scale_mismatch). The sign flips with position: upstream wetland obviously amplified downstream flood risks while downstream wetland was the part the authors would restore first (ev_flood_hazard_wu23_4); restoring many reaches had no effect on property damages and some worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects (ev_flood_hazard_gour20_3, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4); headwater wetlands fill during relatively normal summer rain, which spends the capacity they would need for a much larger event, whereas downstream wetlands that stay dry keep that buffering capacity (ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_2, ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_1). Rewetting itself consumes flood storage: raising ditch water levels to meet winter ecological targets cost flood-water storage equivalent to 3% of the median annual flood volume (ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost) — a wet wetland and an empty flood store are competing objectives. Provenance: temperate and high-income, UK, US and Swedish, with a Chinese basin model; the sole lower-middle-income measurement in scope is a reversal, Zimbabwean headwater dambos protected because they are assumed to reduce floods but measured as the principal mechanism of storm-discharge generation (ev_wetflA_acre_dambo_reversal). The benefit is off-plot in every case.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Floodplain and lakebed restoration costs production mainly by bringing wildlife onto nearby farmland: at Poyang Lake, tenant farmers' crops are damaged by migratory birds and other wild animals and they cannot be compensated [ev_wgy_poy_2]. Elsewhere the effect is neutral to positive: Uganda's matched evaluation found a positive but not significant yield change [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5], and reconnecting a creek in Ghana enhanced cattle farming [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2]. Restored wetlands themselves recover slowly: nitrogen storage remained significantly lower than in reference wetlands for 30 y [ev_soil_nitrogen_mm12_4].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The negative weight comes from a single upper-middle-income survey (Poyang) where compensation goes to landowners rather than to the tenants who bear the crop damage, which is a design problem that targeting could fix. The low-income evidence shows no measurable yield loss. The soil-nitrogen shortfall is an ecological recovery finding, not a farm yield.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: The household evidence on restoring floodplains and lakebeds is negative to null where farmland is retired: at Poyang Lake per capita income fell by 0.338 log points while only transfer income rose (ATT 0.717) [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4], and 56.9% of households in the compensation survey said income decreased, attributed to low compensation rates [ev_wgy_poy_1]; the Uganda GCF matched evaluation found no measurable welfare gain, lower total income in some specifications and more distress coping [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_household_income_fp034e_2]. The Rwanda and Uganda figures describe the income households already draw from existing wetlands, which is the opportunity cost of rewetting, not a benefit of it: cultivating reclaimed Cyabayaga wetland contributed $ 1901 U.S. per household per year, 74% of gross margin, against $ 84 U.S. (24%) in Rugeramigozi [ev_wet_hhinc_naba12_1, ev_wet_hhinc_naba12_2]; selling wetland products earned an average household UGX 99,208 (approx. USD 36) a month in Uganda [ev_wet_hhinc_tury13_3]. Households that collect wetland products are 23% more likely to be food insecure [ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_1].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The class and its strongest evidence disagree. Much of the positive weight comes from existing-wetland use (Rwanda cultivation, Uganda product sales, Lao farmers' fish catches near protected zones [ev_wgy_lao_4, ev_wgy_lao_5]), which shows what households stand to lose if restoration restricts access, and from a society-level Vermont avoided-flood-damage ratio [ev_economic_return_gour20_2]. The measured restoration studies (Poyang, Uganda GCF) are negative or null. Where restoration would rewet farmed wetland like Cyabayaga, the household cost could be large; where it protects wetland that households keep using, losses are smaller. Compensation sized to forgone income and paid to the actual users is the design condition.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: The single unit describes rehabilitation of an eroding wetland: at the Manalana wetland in South Africa's Sand River catchment, rehabilitation structures halted actively advancing erosion gullies that would otherwise have continued through the wetland and degraded the entire area (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1).
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: This is a programme narrative from a sustainable-development case study, with no measurement of soil loss, gully extent or sediment, and it concerns gullies cutting through the wetland itself rather than erosion on the farmland around it (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). It describes what the practice is meant to do; a measured finding or a second independent source is needed before it can say how much.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Reinstating wetland hydrology puts the nutrient load back in contact with saturated soil and vegetation, where nitrogen is denitrified or taken up and phosphorus is stored with sediment on the floodplain. Modelled floodplain reconnection and wetland restoration met the watershed's regulatory phosphorus reduction requirement on predicted phosphorus storage in every scenario (ev_nutrient_removal_worl23_5); restoring degraded wetlands raised the water-quality regulating service - retention, removal and breakdown of nutrients - against the degraded state (ev_nutrient_removal_meli14_5); on Moldova's rehabilitated Lapusna wetland, estimated annual retention is about 17 tons of nitrogen and 3.0 tons of phosphorus (ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1); on Bulgaria's restored Belene Island marshes a first, preliminary test indicated reduced nutrients in outflow water (ev_nutrient_removal_bgicr_3); and the wetlands already standing across a continent remove a large nitrogen mass each year, with the limit on that removal being a spatial disconnect between where wetlands sit and where the nitrogen is (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_1). The last is a siting argument from existing wetlands rather than a restoration effect, and it points the same way: target the hotspots.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The sharpest limit is the land type this tool exists to point at. Grouped by land-use history, wetlands restored on formerly drained cropland were the only group whose phosphorus removal was not significantly different from zero, showing instead an insignificant net release of phosphorus (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_7). On that land the phosphorus benefit does not merely shrink, it reverses. The authors attribute the release to restoring without excavating or isolating the phosphorus-rich soil, which makes it a design decision - strip or isolate the legacy-phosphorus horizon, or expect export in the early years - rather than a reason to rule the practice out. The supporting evidence is also weaker than the direction suggests: the floodplain result is modelled, the Moldovan retention is an estimate resting on an assumed annual flow-through, the Bulgarian result is a single preliminary test (ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1, ev_nutrient_removal_bgicr_3), the continental removal figure measures what existing wetlands already do rather than what restoring adds, and the regulating-service gain is measured against a degraded baseline, so it says restoration beats degradation, not that it reaches intact function. Geographically this is the United States, Bulgaria and Moldova plus a global pooled analysis, high-income, upper-middle or mixed, with no low- or lower-middle-income observation.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Wetlands store water from precipitation and release it slowly to the surrounding environment, which can recharge groundwater aquifers and maintain atmospheric water cycles [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. Rewetting restores that storage close to the intervention: across boreo-temperate wetlands, restoration raised groundwater levels by 22 [16, 28] cm near the intervention, against a drawdown of 19 [10, 27] cm caused by drainage [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_rise]. Managed water levels show the same restored store in project settings: active water regulation held May-June levels in Belarus's Zvanets fen mire during 2021-2022 close to the optimal 5-20 cm above ground despite climate-induced changes [ev_wgy_blr_5]; in Lao PDR a weir at the Nongdern wetland raised the farmland able to use wetland water from 37.16 ha to 73.47 ha [ev_wgy_lao_1], and the evaluators conclude that renovating damaged dykes re-established previously dry lakes and water bodies, raising their water level and surface area [ev_wgy_lao_2].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The gain is local and the wider claim is unsupported. The groundwater rise decays exponentially with distance from the restored ditch and is reduced to 50% after 9 [5, 26] m, whereas drainage drawdown still retains 50% at 21 [11, 64] m, so rewetting does not recover the whole area that drainage dried [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_decay]. The body of literature reporting groundwater measurements outside the wetland soil was too limited to allow a reliable evaluation, so the question of effects beyond the wetland was inconclusive [ev_wetflA_bring_outside_inconclusive]: a claim that rewetting raises groundwater under neighbouring farmland is not supported here. Catchment storage is contested: a fieldwork-based study found no significant increase in floodplain water storage or overland flow, while modelling showed a 6-fold increase in overland flow storage volume [ev_wetflA_zhu_restoration_variability]. The null units are convergence with an intact reference rather than failure of the intervention: hydrological features of restored and created wetlands appeared recovered immediately against reference wetlands, though followed for only 10 y to 15 y [ev_water_regulation_mm12_5], and hydrological dynamics and water quality showed full recovery [ev_water_regulation_meli14_7]. The Ramsar line is a general functional statement about wetlands rather than a restoration measurement [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. The groundwater measurements are all temperate or boreal and high-income or unspecified. The one unit that measures water reaching farmland is the Lao weir — water-control infrastructure inside a Ramsar wetland, measured as area served before and after construction, not as groundwater beyond the wetland [ev_wgy_lao_1]; the dyke result is the evaluators' conclusion rather than a measurement [ev_wgy_lao_2]; and the Belarus levels are held by active regulation and last only while it continues [ev_wgy_blr_5].

wetland_management__rural_poverty.mechanism: Wetland restoration reaches household income mainly through compensation and payment schemes, not through the restored wetland itself; where those payments are too small or go to the wrong people, households lose. At Poyang Lake, households that returned farmland to the lake gained only transfer income in the matched comparison (ATT 0.717 on log transfer income) while per capita income fell by 0.338 log points [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2]; the authors report a significant negative impact on household income [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_6], no longer significant by the later panel round [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_7]. A separate Poyang compensation survey found 56.9% of households said income decreased after joining the policy, 38.3% no change and only 4.8% an increase, which the authors attribute to low compensation rates [ev_wgy_poy_1]. In Uganda, the Green Climate Fund evaluation, the only matched-counterfactual household study of this practice in a low-income country, found that early changes did not translate into measurable improvements in income, assets or food security; treated households reported lower total income in some specifications (significant at the 10 per cent level) and more distress coping [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_household_income_fp034e_2, ev_household_income_fp034e_3, ev_food_security_fp034e_4]. On drained peat, paludiculture is generally not profitable at farm level when revenue relies solely on biomass sales [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1], and SE Asian oil palm communities face lower returns under rewetting [ev_household_income_mish21_5]. In Belarus, evaluators found no evidence of direct benefit to ordinary people, but the design contained no household mechanism, so this records the absence of a designed benefit, not a tested null [ev_wgy_blr_1].
wetland_management__rural_poverty.conditionality: This is a finding about how restoration is paid for, not a verdict on wetlands. The household gains in the pool come from wages on restoration works and from compensation: Working for Wetlands in South Africa employed long-term unemployed people [ev_household_income_bbr_3], and at Manalana provisioning benefits of R2 million against R1 million in costs to 34 households over 50 years [ev_economic_return_bbr_2]; high-value niche products (Sphagnum founder material, thatching reed) can be profitable [ev_wet_econret_neud26_2, ev_wgy_wich_6]. Much of the positive economic evidence is society-level, not household: the Vermont 5-to-1 benefit-cost ratio counts avoided flood damage [ev_economic_return_gour20_2], and about 40% of salt marsh projects recover cost within 30 years [ev_economic_return_wang22_5]. In Kabale, Uganda, the national wetland policy had little impact on household incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_1]. Where an investment sizes compensation to the forgone farm income and pays the people who actually farm the land, the direction could differ, but no study in the pool shows it.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__aez-h.mechanism: Both units concern wet use of tropical peat and they are, in substance, the same finding seen from opposite ends. Tan et al. conclude from net present value, internal rate of return and benefit-cost ratio that paludiculture may generate a small margin of economic benefit, while stating in the same breath that its economic benefits relative to conventional drainage-based crops are still too low and that not all paludiculture costs and externalities are documented in the economics analyses [ev_economic_return_tan21_10]. Mishra et al. put the same gap from the household side: communities that have relied on oil palm cultivation will find it challenging to participate in peatland restoration, since rewetting may entail lower productivity and financial return for their crops [ev_household_income_mish21_5].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__aez-h.conditionality: The class reads as a reduction in rural poverty, and the units do not establish that. Both are reviews citing other work; neither measures a household, and neither attaches a magnitude. The positive unit is a modelled margin that the same sentence qualifies as too small against the drained alternative, and the negative unit is a reversal — the adopting household loses income. Taken together they describe a practice whose return sits below the land use it replaces, which is a reason to expect compensation or a payment mechanism to be necessary, not a reason to expect poverty to fall. Both studies are Indonesian and Malaysian upper-middle-income settings, so a low- or lower-middle-income humid-tropics investment has no directly applicable evidence here.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__farmi.mechanism: Where rainfed cropland is withdrawn for restoration, household income falls unless payments replace the lost harvest. The Poyang Lake panel shows per capita income down by 0.338 log points and transfer income up (ATT 0.717) for households that returned farmland to the lake [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4], with the authors reporting a significant negative impact on income [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_6]. In Kabale, Uganda, the wetland policy had little impact on household incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_1]. The positive cases are employment-based: Working for Wetlands paid previously unemployed people to rehabilitate wetlands, with R2 million of provisioning benefits against R1 million of costs to 34 households at Manalana [ev_economic_return_bbr_2, ev_household_income_bbr_3].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__farmi.conditionality: The Poyang study dominates the weight, so this row mostly describes an upper-middle-income lakebed-retirement programme without continuous subsidy; most of the pool's weight is from outside the low-income target. The Poyang loss faded to non-significance years after the policy began [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_7]. The South African gain is a wage channel from public works, not income from the restored wetland.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.mechanism: In high-income settings farm households are made whole mainly by payments or by niche markets. Paludiculture is generally not profitable at farm level on biomass sales alone [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1], it is challenging to keep income at the level of conventional agriculture [ev_wet_econret_temm26_4], and seasonal water-table raising restricts management in ways that reduce farm income [ev_household_income_cxc_5]. Reed for bioenergy ranges from a loss of around £870 ha−1 yr−1 to a profit of £1300 ha−1 yr−1 depending on harvest option [ev_economic_return_cxc_6]. Farmed Sphagnum cannot compete with peat as a growing medium at 25 € [ev_wgy_wich_4], is viable for orchid cultivation only at medium to high yields [ev_wgy_wich_5], and is profitable as founder material even in the most pessimistic scenario [ev_wgy_wich_6]; thatching reed and directly marketed water buffalo products can also pay [ev_wet_econret_neud26_2].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.conditionality: The class and the strongest farm-level evidence disagree. The moderate positive leans on a modelled 5-to-1 benefit-cost ratio of avoided flood damage in Vermont, which is a community property benefit [ev_economic_return_gour20_2], on an asserted SDG mapping that land-users maintain income through biomass and nature-based payments 'if available' [ev_wet_hhinc_temm26_6], and on niche Sphagnum markets. The farm-level reviews say the opposite for mainstream biomass. Society-level returns (salt marsh projects recovering cost within 30 years in about 40% of cases [ev_economic_return_wang22_5]; marsh defences from just as expensive to around three times cheaper than breakwaters [ev_economic_return_nara16_6], and not always cost effective [ev_economic_return_nara16_5]) do not reach farm income without a payment. Read as: restoration pays society; farmers come out ahead only with a payment or a niche product.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.mechanism: The matched evidence in low-income settings shows no household gain. The Uganda GCF evaluation found that awareness, crop diversification and adaptation changes did not translate into measurable improvements in income, assets or food security; total income was lower among treated households, significant at the 10 per cent level, while crop-farming income was close to zero difference and food-security indicators showed no significant difference [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_household_income_fp034e_2, ev_household_income_fp034e_3, ev_food_security_fp034e_4]. In Kabale, Uganda, the national wetland policy had little impact on household incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_1]; 43% of respondents earned UGX 10,000-100,000 per year from the wetland [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_2] and 22% earned nothing from it, leaving no incentive to conserve [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_3].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.conditionality: The class and its strongest evidence disagree. The slight positive comes from Kabale households' income from using the wetland, which measures dependence on an existing resource rather than an effect of restoration, and from an Uzbek project completion report asserting a substantial increase in income from fish, muskrat skin and reeds that it did not directly measure [ev_household_income_uzicr_1]. The only matched-counterfactual study finds a null with lower total income. Treat restoration in low-income settings as income-neutral to negative unless the design adds an adequate, well-targeted livelihood payment.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings household losses follow the land taken out of farming and the size of compensation. At Poyang Lake, households that returned farmland to the lake gained transfer income (ATT 0.717) while per capita income fell by 0.338 log points [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2], and 56.9% of surveyed households said income decreased after joining the compensation policy, attributed to low compensation rates [ev_wgy_poy_1]. In SE Asia, communities relying on oil palm face lower productivity and financial return under rewetting [ev_household_income_mish21_5], and tropical paludiculture yields only a small margin of economic benefit, still too low against drainage-based crops [ev_economic_return_tan21_10]. Gains come from employment on restoration works in South Africa [ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_economic_return_bbr_2] and, in Belarus, from indirect ecotourism and berry marketing benefits that did not reach vulnerable groups [ev_wgy_blr_2].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.conditionality: The Belarus null records the absence of any designed household mechanism, not a tested effect of rewetting on income [ev_wgy_blr_1]. The Chinese high-altitude peatland claim that restoration helps alleviate poverty is an editorial forward reference, not a measured result [ev_rural_poverty_bonn16_3]. The Poyang income losses became non-significant by the later panel round as households re-based their livelihoods [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_7], so the loss is largest in the years after restoration. Compensation size and who receives it are the levers.

wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk.mechanism: Vegetation and standing water hold sediment in place. In coastal marsh, planting raises accretion and surface elevation and reduces lateral erosion against a degraded shore (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3); on a disturbed peatland, drain-blocking is reported, citing the literature, to generally lead to a substantial reduction in the outflow of suspended solids (ev_wgy_ram_7); in South Africa's Manalana wetland, rehabilitation structures halted the advance of erosion gullies that would otherwise have continued through the wetland and degraded the entire area (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1); inland, a wetland set in the flow path intercepts sediment carried through it, which is the service whose decline is recorded here (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5).
wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk.conditionality: This row pools comparisons that do not share a denominator, and the class should be read as weak and heterogeneous rather than as an erosion measurement. The measured positive unit is a coastal shoreline-protection effect size measured against degraded marsh (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3), on a scale the source does not define. The negative unit is not measured erosion at all but a created inland wetland whose sediment retention was diminishing after a decade of river flow (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5) - a decaying trapping service, not soil being lost from a field. The null is a blanket-peat restoration in which the share of storm rainfall becoming storm discharge did not change at either restored site relative to the bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null); that paper's own conclusion is that restoration shifted the timing and peak of delivery rather than the volume, so it is a runoff-volume result standing in for an erosion claim. The Manalana gully result is a programme narrative without a measurement, and it concerns gullies cutting through the wetland itself rather than soil loss from surrounding fields (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1); the Ramsar statement is a cited synthesis about suspended solids leaving drained peat, not erosion on farmland (ev_wgy_ram_7). Nothing in the pool measures soil loss on farmland, and apart from the South African case all of it comes from high-income temperate coastal and upland settings.

wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk__f.mechanism: A wetland in a farmed catchment can hold soil in two ways: rehabilitation structures stop gullies cutting into the wetland, and a wetland in the flow path traps sediment carried from upstream. In South Africa's Manalana wetland, rehabilitation halted actively advancing erosion gullies that would otherwise have continued through the wetland and degraded the entire area (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). At created riverine wetlands in Ohio, the trapping service is what the evidence tracks, and there are some signs that sediment and total phosphorus retention are diminishing after 10 years of river flow (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5).
wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk__f.conditionality: Neither unit measures soil loss on cropland, and the adverse direction of this row comes from the Ohio unit, which records a trapping service weakening with age, not a wetland adding erosion: the basins were still retaining sediment, with nitrate and soluble reactive phosphorus retention holding, so the finding is that sediment trapping cannot be assumed to last without maintenance (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5). The South African unit points the other way but is a programme narrative without a measurement, about gullies in the wetland itself (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). Read together they say a wetland can protect itself from gullying and can trap sediment for a decade or so; they say nothing about erosion on the surrounding rainfed fields.

wetland_management__water_quality_risk.mechanism: The service is physical and biological at once: water is made to pass slowly through a created or restored wetland, sediment settles, plants take up nutrients and denitrification removes nitrogen. Across the created and restored wetlands reviewed, median removal rates were 93 g of total nitrogen and 1.2 g of total phosphorus per square metre per year [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_1, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_2], median removal efficiency was 37% of the incoming nitrogen load (95% confidence interval 29-44%) and 46% of the phosphorus load (37-55%) [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_4], and the review's own summary is that created wetlands generally remove both and that overall removal efficiency is roughly 40% [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_5]. Measured on created riverine basins, nitrate removal was 42% in the tenth year and soluble reactive phosphorus retention stayed around 70% [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2]. Against the realistic counterfactual the same holds: restoration raised the water-quality regulating service by 31% over degraded wetlands [ev_nutrient_removal_meli14_5], and nutrient and carbon loads were lower from restored peat extraction sites than from abandoned ones [ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5]. Where the wetlands are put multiplies all of this: a spatially targeted increase in United States wetland area by 10 per cent would double wetland nitrogen removal [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2] and give an estimated 54 per cent decrease in nitrogen loading in nitrate-affected watersheds [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3], and placing wetlands where the nitrogen surplus is highest provides approximately 40 times more removal than placing them on non-agricultural land, at nearly double the cost [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4], with removal rising linearly up to roughly a 15% increase in wetland area before targeting runs out of high-surplus land [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_5]. Floodplain reconnection and wetland restoration scenarios met a watershed's required phosphorus load reduction on predicted storage [ev_nutrient_removal_worl23_5], and designing for nitrogen retention did not cost species richness [ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6]. Project and synthesis sources add the same direction in other settings. On Moldova's rehabilitated Lapusna wetland, estimated annual retention is about 17 tons of nitrogen and 3.0 tons of phosphorus, from inlet and outlet concentrations and an assumed mean annual flow-through [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1]; on Bulgaria's restored Belene Island marshes a first, preliminary test indicated a reduction in nutrients in outflow water [ev_nutrient_removal_bgicr_3]; and the Ramsar technical report, citing the literature, states that disturbed peatlands release substantial quantities of humic acids, nitrogen, sulphur, heavy metals and suspended solids, whereas drain-blocking generally leads to a substantial reduction in their outflow [ev_wgy_ram_6, ev_wgy_ram_7].
wetland_management__water_quality_risk.conditionality: The setting a rural scan would target is the setting where the phosphorus side of this can reverse. Total phosphorus removal was significantly different from zero for every wetland-history group except wetlands restored on formerly drained cropland, for which there was an insignificant net release of phosphorus [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_7]; negative phosphorus removal rates were reported in 17 of 146 wetlands, six of them created on former cropland and one on previous cattle pasture, whose soil is usually rich in phosphorus that may be released after construction [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_6]. An annual release rather than removal of nitrogen appears in a very small number of studies, while negative phosphorus rates are less uncommon [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_9], and in 17 individual cases the confidence limits encompassed the zero-effect line, including one whose average indicated a release of nitrogen [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_8]. Rewetting peat carries its own reversals, both from the Ramsar report's cited synthesis: in some cases restoration causes a temporarily increased flush of nutrients into downstream water courses, though the release decreases in the longer term [ev_wgy_ram_8]; and on nutrient-rich, formerly fertilised agricultural fens rewetting may even increase the nutrient problem by mobilising hitherto bound phosphorus and nitrogen, called internal eutrophication [ev_wgy_ram_9]. A rural scan aimed at farmed peat should expect both. Age is the second condition: in the tenth year after construction total phosphorus decreased by only 2% in one basin and increased by 14% in the other, after a consistent pattern of retention during the first 8 years [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4], and sediment and total phosphorus retention showed signs of diminishing after 10 years of river flow even while nitrate and soluble reactive phosphorus retention held [ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5]. Not every restoration touches water quality at all: blocking gullies on an eroding upland peatland had no significant positive impact on water quality and left a non-significant increase in dissolved organic carbon [ev_wetflA_gatis_waterquality_null]. Finally, the largest numbers in the row are modelled national scenarios rather than measurements [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4], the efficiencies vary with hydraulic loading and temperature, the inflows behind them include treated wastewater and urban runoff as well as agricultural runoff [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3], the Moldovan retention is an estimate built on an assumed flow-through, the Bulgarian result is a single preliminary test with further monitoring said to be needed [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1, ev_nutrient_removal_bgicr_3], and every quantified unit comes from Europe or North America.

wetland_management__water_quality_risk__.mechanism: In rainfed cropping catchments a wetland works as an interception point for the nutrients leaving the fields. In the 10th year after construction, average nitrate removal by the created riverine basins was 42%, the highest of the decade [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1], and soluble reactive phosphorus retention continued to be significant at around 70%, 63% in the planted basin and 73% in the naturally colonising one, with no significant difference between them [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2]. In Swedish farmland, nutrient retention and diversity proved compatible aims, since biodiversity was neither locally nor regionally harmed by high nitrate levels [ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6].
wetland_management__water_quality_risk__.conditionality: Phosphorus is where this fails. By the 10th year total phosphorus showed little retention and even export, falling by only 2% in the naturally colonising basin and rising by 14% in the planted one, after a consistent pattern of retention over the first 8 years [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4]: the created wetland had become a net phosphorus exporter in its tenth year. Sediment and total phosphorus retention were diminishing after 10 years of river flow [ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5], so the particulate fraction of the service decays as the basin fills while the dissolved-nutrient service persists. Both studies sit in temperate, high-income rainfed cropland, Ohio and Sweden, and both concern created wetlands fed by river or catchment water rather than restored ones; the Ohio basins were continuously pumped, which is not how a wetland in a farmed catchment is fed. Nothing was measured in a tropical or lower-income rainfed system.

wetland_management__water_stress.mechanism: A wetland stores water from precipitation and releases it slowly to its surroundings, which can recharge groundwater aquifers [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]; rewetting a drained wetland restores that store by putting the water table back. Across the boreal and temperate evidence, restoration increased groundwater levels by 22 cm near the intervention, with a confidence interval of 16 to 28 cm, against the 19 cm drawdown that drainage had caused [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_rise]; because the effects of restoration and drainage were of similar magnitude and opposite direction, rewetting of drained peatlands can on average be expected to restore groundwater levels near the ditch [ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. The same is observed on the ground: mean water tables rose significantly at all distance classes after an Exmoor peatland was restored, from just below the surface to above it in the peat pans [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable], and the water-table level of drained peat extraction sites was reported to be successfully recovered by active restoration through ditch blocking and dam construction [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_6]. Project evaluations add managed-water cases. In Belarus, active water regulation held May-June water levels in the Zvanets fen mire during 2021-2022 close to the optimal 5-20 cm above ground despite climate-induced changes in the Polesie region [ev_wgy_blr_5]. In Lao PDR the evidence is engineered rather than restorative: a weir at the Nongdern wetland raised the farmland able to use wetland water from 37.16 ha to 73.47 ha, almost 100 percent [ev_wgy_lao_1], and the evaluators conclude that renovating damaged dykes re-established previously dry lakes and water bodies, raising their water level and surface area for the dry season and other livelihood activities [ev_wgy_lao_2].
wetland_management__water_stress.conditionality: The footprint is the problem, and it is small. The groundwater rise decayed exponentially with distance from the restored ditch and was reduced to 50% after 9 m, with a confidence interval of 5 to 26 m, whereas drainage drawdown reached considerably farther and was still at 50% at 21 m [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_decay] — so restoration may not reach all the area affected by drainage, and the result depends strongly on local context [ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. Beyond the wetland itself the evidence runs out: the body of literature reporting groundwater measurements outside the wetland soil was limited and did not allow a reliable evaluation, leaving the question inconclusive [ev_wetflA_bring_outside_inconclusive]. Any expectation that rewetting a wetland raises groundwater under neighbouring farmland is therefore unsupported here, and this row should be read as a change inside and immediately around the wetland. Nor does the hydrology come back whole. Water-table fluctuation and the moisture dynamics of the peat layer were found difficult to maintain in restored extraction areas, so the level can be restored while its dynamics are not [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7]; many hydrological processes do not fully recover within the initial few years after restoration because of earlier changes in peat structure and consolidation caused by degradation [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]; at Exmoor the median water-table condition remained similar at all distances, so the significant rise is in the mean and driven by the wettest states rather than by a shift in the typical state [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]; and restoration results vary enough that fieldwork found no significant increase in floodplain water storage or overland flow where modelling showed a 6-fold increase in overland-flow storage volume [ev_wetflA_zhu_restoration_variability]. The groundwater and water-table sources are concentrated in Canada, Finland, Estonia, Ireland, Germany, Great Britain, Sweden and the United States, and the practice behind them is peatland ditch blocking in boreal and temperate landscapes — the relevance of these numbers to a dryland farming system is untested. The only unit that measures water reaching farmland is the Lao weir, which is water-control infrastructure in a Ramsar wetland: its gain is in area served, measured before and after the weir, and says nothing about groundwater beyond the wetland [ev_wgy_lao_1]; the dyke renovation result is the evaluators' conclusion, not a measurement [ev_wgy_lao_2]; and the Belarus water levels are held by active regulation, so they depend on that regulation continuing [ev_wgy_blr_5].

wetland_management__water_stress__income.mechanism: In the high-income boreo-temperate evidence, rewetting measurably puts water back where the drain took it from. Across boreo-temperate wetlands, restoration raised groundwater levels by 22 [16, 28] cm near the intervention, against a drawdown of 19 [10, 27] cm caused by drainage, so the effects of restoration and drainage were of similar magnitude and opposite direction and rewetting a drained peatland can on average be expected to restore groundwater levels near the ditch [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_rise, ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. On an eroding English upland peatland, peat barriers across gullies raised mean water tables significantly at all distance classes, in the peat pans from 0.003 m below ground level to 0.064 m above it and in the vegetated haggs from 0.188 to 0.175 m below ground within 0.5 m of the pan edge [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. On cutaway peat, the water-table level was successfully recovered by active restoration through ditch blocking and dam construction [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_6].
wetland_management__water_stress__income.conditionality: The footprint is small and the recovery is partial. The groundwater rise decays exponentially with distance from the restored ditch and is reduced to 50% after 9 [5, 26] m, whereas drainage drawdown still retains 50% at 21 [11, 64] m, so restoration may not reach all the area drainage affected, with a strong dependence on local context [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_decay, ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. The body of literature reporting groundwater measurements outside the wetland soil was too limited for a reliable evaluation, leaving effects beyond the wetland inconclusive [ev_wetflA_bring_outside_inconclusive]. The English rise is in the mean rather than the typical state: median water-table conditions remained similar at all distances after restoration, so the significant mean rise is driven by the wet tail [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. Water-table fluctuation and the moisture dynamics of the peat layer were difficult to maintain in restored peat-extraction areas, so the level returns but its dynamics do not [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7]. Catchment storage is contested: a fieldwork-based study found no significant increase in floodplain water storage or overland flow, while modelling showed a 6-fold increase in overland flow storage volume, and the fieldwork study is itself cited within this review rather than independent of it [ev_wetflA_zhu_restoration_variability]. Every unit is temperate or boreal and high-income, from the UK, Ireland, Fennoscandia, Canada and northern Europe, and none measures water available to a farming system.

wetland_management__water_stress__income.mechanism: The direction in this scope rests on the general hydrological function rather than on a measured restoration: wetlands store water from precipitation and slowly release it to the surrounding environment, which can recharge groundwater aquifers and maintain atmospheric water cycles [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. Restoring or protecting a wetland is expected to restore that storage and slow release, and so to ease a water deficit downstream of it.
wetland_management__water_stress__income.conditionality: This cell is thin, and its units pull in different directions. The positive unit is a functional statement about wetlands in general, offered as a key message rather than as the measured result of any restoration, with no magnitude, no time to effect and no country attached [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. The other is a timescale caveat from a narrative review: numerous studies of peatland rewetting suggest that many hydrological processes do not fully recover within the initial few years after restoration, because of earlier changes in peat structure and consolidation caused by degradation [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]. That caveat cuts both ways — short monitoring windows may hide a benefit as easily as they may flatter an early result — but it means nothing here establishes what a restored wetland delivers, to whom, or when. Nothing in this scope measures a farm-level water supply, and neither unit names the income context it was observed in; treat the direction as an expectation to be tested in the pilot rather than as evidence of a delivered gain.

wetland_management__waterlogging__all.mechanism: Rewetting raises the water table in the peat, and the water does not stop at the project boundary. The Ramsar technical guidance on peatland rewetting sets two design constraints on this: where adjacent land use may be impaired, rewetting must be done gradually and flooding of surrounding land must be avoided (ev_wgy_ram_15); and where downward seepage is diffuse, elevating the water table in a residual peat massif will require raising the water level in the surrounding land, farmland included (ev_wgy_ram_16). The first treats waterlogging of neighbouring land as a risk to be managed; the second describes a setting where wetting neighbouring farmland is built into the method.
wetland_management__waterlogging__all.conditionality: These are design constraints stated by an authority, not measurements. Neither statement says how often neighbouring land is waterlogged, by how much, for how long, or what it costs the farmers who work it, and both come from one advocacy-adjacent guidance document; they establish that the risk is recognised, not its size or frequency, and they should not be read as evidence that rewetting routinely floods farmland. Unlike the flood benefits elsewhere in this recipe, the cost here falls on the neighbouring farm household rather than downstream. For scoping, a rewetting proposal adjacent to farmland should plan for gradual water-level raising, identify the adjacent parcels whose water level the design may depend on, and treat any need to raise water on those parcels as something to agree with their users before the works, not an incidental side effect. No country, income group, climate zone or farming system is attached to either statement.

wetland_management__wind_cyclone__all.mechanism: This cell carries no measured wind or cyclone mechanism. Its sole unit is a caution about the asset rather than a protective effect: a replacement wetland may take decades to fully develop the functions provided by the original wetland (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_7). Whatever storm-protection function an established coastal wetland performs, the evidence here says a newly restored or created wetland does not perform it from the outset.
wetland_management__wind_cyclone__all.conditionality: Direction in this cell rests on an expert statement in the discussion section of a US study, not on a measurement, and it concerns compensatory replacement wetlands rather than any practice sited in a rural landscape. There is no quantified wind or cyclone outcome in scope, no non-high-income setting, and no farm-level beneficiary — the protection at issue is of coastal property. Treat the row as a marker for evidence not yet gathered, carrying a single usable implication: an establishment lag of decades before any protective function can be credited to the works.
